meta.name: HowDoesThisLand persuasion model
meta.description: A standalone data model for judging persuasive content through Aristotle's modes of persuasion (pisteis) plus kairos, operationalised with modern influence, behavioural and narrative research, and held to a standard of persuasion that builds trust and examined conviction.
meta.derived_from: Gumption knowledge base (frameworks, concepts, thinkers, studies) plus an evidence register of research checked for this version. All grounded_in ids resolve to knowledge_refs; research ids resolve to research.
changes_from_0_1: Kairos promoted to a fourth core appeal with five dimensions; urgency moved out of pathos
Telos lens refocused on one clear purpose
Audience archetypes and executive role profiles
Craft metrics: readability, passive voice, emotional language, devices, appeal share by words
Evidence register; moves corrected where research disagrees
Two new content types and two new red flags
meta.heuristic_conventions: heuristic and quick patterns are JavaScript regular expressions applied per sentence with flags gimu; a leading (?c) means case-sensitive. target_per_k = signals per 1,000 words for a top score.
changes_from_0_2: Previous function set replaced by five rhetorical duties grounded in Cicero's officia oratoris and Aristotle's deliberative aim
Audience archetypes rebuilt on need for cognition, regulatory focus and persuasion knowledge; a fifth archetype (The Sceptic) added
Executive role profiles rewritten and extended to 14 roles, including procurement and board members
Third-party benchmarks and phrasing replaced with primary sources (Gunning, Kinneavy, Higgins & Walker)

New critical-suspicion perspective (Nietzsche, motivated reasoning) with six levers
Flourishing (eudaimonia) lever in the ethics perspective
Three new moves: invite a response, say what would change your mind, declare your interest

Reader expertise setting and length targets by content type
Ten new evidence-register entries on culture, cohesion and plain language

appeals.name: Ethos
appeals.question: Why should this audience believe this speaker?
appeals.aristotle: Persuasion through the character of the speaker, made credible by the speech itself. Aristotle names three sources: practical wisdom (phronesis), virtue (arete) and goodwill (eunoia).
appeals.modern_reading: Credibility, trust and identification. Modern research splits it into competence and warmth (Fiske), and the Trust Equation adds reliability and low self-orientation. In Greek thought persuasion (peithō) and trust (pistis) are bound together: people are persuaded by those they trust, and trust is earned through character.

appeals.name: Pathos
appeals.question: Why should this audience care, and feel moved to act?
appeals.aristotle: Persuasion by putting the audience into a certain frame of mind. Emotions change judgement, so the speaker must understand what the audience feels, towards whom, and why.
appeals.modern_reading: Motivation, stakes and meaning. Covers pain and desire, loss framing, story, identity and status, and the felt sense of being understood.

appeals.name: Logos
appeals.question: Why should this audience think it is true and makes sense?
appeals.aristotle: Persuasion through the argument itself, by proof or apparent proof. Aristotle's rhetorical proof is the enthymeme: an argument that leaves premises the audience already holds unstated.
appeals.modern_reading: Evidence, mechanism, structure and clarity. Includes the reason why, comparison with alternatives, and handling objections before they are raised.

appeals.name: Kairos
appeals.question: Why this, why now, and why should the audience act?
appeals.aristotle: The opportune moment. Greek rhetoric treated timeliness and fitness to the occasion as part of persuasion; later teaching often neglected it.
appeals.modern_reading: Timeliness, stakes of delay, efficacy and the call to act. Urgency persuades when it is genuine and paired with a feasible path; urgency without a way out tends to overwhelm.

dimensions.name: Competence and judgement
dimensions.description: Shows the author knows what they are doing: relevant experience, track record, specific results and sound judgement about the reader's situation.
judge_asks: What evidence of relevant expertise is in the text itself?
Are achievements specific, or just job titles and adjectives?
Does the author show judgement (diagnosis, trade-offs), not just claim it?

rubric.1: Expertise is asserted with adjectives or titles only.
rubric.4: Specific, quantified track record plus visible judgement about the reader's problem.

positive_signals: Years and scope of relevant experience
Diagnostic insight about the reader's world
Credentials that matter to this audience

dimensions.name: Integrity and candour
dimensions.description: Reads as honest: claims are proportionate, limits are admitted, risk is shared, and nothing is inflated. Candour often raises credibility (pratfall effect), but only when a raised weakness is then answered.
judge_asks: Are claims proportionate to the evidence offered?
Does the author admit limits, trade-offs or who it is not for?
Is there skin in the game (guarantee, commitment) where appropriate?

rubric.3: Proportionate claims with some candour or risk-sharing.
rubric.4: Visibly honest: admits limits, qualifies claims, shares risk, says who it is not for.

positive_signals: Guarantee or risk reversal that is real
negative_signals: Claims the author cannot back up

pos: \b(not for everyone|isn't for you|is not for|we don't|we do not|we won't)\b
\b(risks?:|alternatives considered|the hard part|i'?ll start with|to be honest|i know this)\b

dimensions.name: Goodwill and reader focus
dimensions.description: The author is visibly on the reader's side: talks about their world, not the author's ego. Low self-orientation is the strongest single driver of trust in the Trust Equation.
judge_asks: Is the text mostly about the reader or about the author?
Does it make the reader the hero and the author the guide?
Does it give value before asking?

rubric.1: Mostly self-focused; reader is an afterthought.
rubric.4: Clearly serves the reader first, gives value up front, and frames the author as guide.

positive_signals: 'You' language anchored in the reader's situation
Customer as hero, author as guide

dimensions.name: Borrowed credibility
dimensions.description: Third parties vouch for the author: testimonials, client names, reviews, media, endorsements, certifications. Social proof works best when the reference group resembles the reader.
judge_asks: Who, other than the author, vouches for this?
Is the proof specific (named, quantified) and relevant to this reader?
Does the social proof come from people like the reader?

rubric.4: Rich, specific proof from people like the reader, tied to outcomes.

positive_signals: Press or awards relevant to the reader
negative_signals: Logos with no link to outcomes
Proof from an irrelevant reference group

pos: \b(testimonials?|trusted by|used by|clients? (include|such as)|customers? (include|like)|featured (in|on)|as seen (in|on)|rated|reviews?|★|stars?|case stud(y|ies)|recommended by|partnered with|endorsed)\b

dimensions.name: Identification and shared identity
dimensions.description: The reader feels the author is one of them: shared background, language, values or struggle. Cialdini's unity and liking; Godin's 'people like us'.
judge_asks: Does the author signal shared identity or experience with the reader?
Does the language sound like the reader's own?
Are shared values made explicit?

rubric.0: Author feels alien to the reader.
rubric.4: Strong, authentic 'one of us' signal that fits the audience.

negative_signals: Corporate voice to an individual reader
Jargon from the author's world, not the reader's

pos: \b(like you|people like (us|you)|i('ve| have) been (there|where you)|we('ve| have) been there|i was once|fellow|our community|as a (founder|parent|engineer|marketer|leader|manager|designer|developer|owner))\b

dimensions.name: Polish and consistency
dimensions.description: Professional presentation: consistent tone, no errors or shouting, appropriate formality. Sloppiness is read as a signal about competence (thin slicing, halo effect).
judge_asks: Are there errors, inconsistencies or formatting problems?
Is the register consistent and appropriate to the audience?
Does anything look unfinished?

rubric.1: Several errors or jarring tone shifts.
rubric.4: Flawless, with a consistent and distinctive voice.

dimensions.name: Stakes: pain and desire
dimensions.description: Names what the reader is struggling with and what they want. The push of the current situation and the pull of a better one (JTBD forces, PAS, the gap).
judge_asks: Is the reader's problem named in terms they would recognise?
Is the desired outcome vivid and desirable?
Is the gap between them made felt?

rubric.1: Problem or desire is vague or generic.
rubric.2: Problem or outcome named but not felt.
rubric.3: Clear, recognisable pain and desirable outcome.
rubric.4: The reader's struggling moment and dream outcome are named so precisely they feel seen.

positive_signals: Consequence of the problem made concrete

pos: \b(late or not at all|walks? \d+|every morning|afraid|quit within)\b

dimensions.name: Concreteness and vividness
dimensions.description: Concrete, sensory, specific language the reader can picture. Abstract corporate language does not move anyone (Made to Stick: Concrete; curse of knowledge).
judge_asks: Can the reader picture what is described?
Are there specific moments, places, people or objects?
How much abstract jargon is there?

rubric.4: Vivid, sensory, specific throughout; easy to picture.

pos: \b(at night|midnight|the night before|first thing|tomorrow morning|late at night)\b

dimensions.name: Story and narrative
dimensions.description: Uses narrative: a character, a problem, a turning point and a result. Stories transport readers and lower resistance (Hall, StoryBrand, epiphany bridge, STAR).
judge_asks: Is there a story, even a short one?
Does it have a character the reader relates to, tension and a resolution?
Does the story carry the point, or decorate it?

rubric.2: A story is present but flat or generic.
rubric.3: A clear story with tension and resolution.
rubric.4: A compelling story that carries the argument and makes the reader the hero.

negative_signals: Company history recited as a timeline
Story about the author's ego with no reader relevance

dimensions.name: Identity, status and belonging
dimensions.description: Connects the action to who the reader is or wants to be: status, belonging, pride, social currency. 'People like us do things like this.'
judge_asks: Does acting on this say something good about the reader?
Is there an aspirational identity or group to join?
Would sharing it give the reader social currency?

rubric.3: Clear identity or belonging appeal fitted to the reader.
rubric.4: Powerful identity appeal that makes acting feel like being true to oneself.

negative_signals: Status threat to the reader's current choice (makes them look wrong)

pos: \b(we have done|we can do|together|one of you|each of you)\b

dimensions.name: Empathy and emotional resonance
dimensions.description: Shows the author understands how the reader feels and sets an emotional tone that fits. Labelling feelings, accusation audits and warmth (Voss, Duhigg, Carnegie).
judge_asks: Does the author name or acknowledge the reader's feelings?
Is the emotional tone right for the audience and moment?
Is emotion earned, or laid on?

rubric.3: Clear empathy with a fitting tone.
rubric.4: The reader feels deeply understood; emotion is earned and well judged.

positive_signals: Acknowledging doubts before they are raised

pos: \b(we (know|understand|get it)|you might (feel|be feeling)|it can feel|it'?s (hard|not easy|tough|frustrating)|you('re| are) not alone|sounds like|no wonder|that'?s understandable|we('ve| have) heard|(they|clients|customers) told us)\b
\b(i know this is|unsettling|some of you (will|may) feel|you('ll| will) feel|i understand|personally)\b

dimensions.name: Surprise, humour and delight
dimensions.description: Something unexpected: a twist, a reframe, a moment of humour or wonder. Surprise is the emotion most able to shift a set mindset, and humour aids attention and memory (Made to Stick: Unexpected; the Entertain function).
judge_asks: Is there anything the reader would not have predicted?
Is there a moment of lightness, wit or wonder that fits the setting?
Would the reader want to know what happens next?

rubric.3: A genuine surprise or well-judged humour that serves the point.
rubric.4: Surprise and delight that make the core idea memorable and keep the reader leaning in.

negative_signals: Clickbait gaps that are never paid off

pos: \b(surpris\w*|turns out|here'?s the thing|counter-?intuitive|what if|it'?s not what you think|the opposite|believe it or not|oddly|ironically|plot twist)\b
neg: \b(think outside the box|at the end of the day|game-?changer|low-?hanging fruit|move the needle|circle back)\b

dimensions.name: Specific claims and evidence
dimensions.description: Claims are specific and backed: numbers, data, named examples, sources. Specificity is more believable than generality (Hopkins, Ogilvy).
judge_asks: Are the main claims specific and quantified?
Is evidence offered for them (data, examples, sources)?
Are there vague or weasel claims?

rubric.4: Every key claim is specific, quantified where possible, and sourced.

dimensions.name: Mechanism and reasoning
dimensions.description: Explains why and how: the reason why, the unique mechanism, cause and effect. Even weak reasons raise compliance for small asks; big asks need real ones.
judge_asks: Does the text explain how the result is achieved?
Are causal links stated ('because', 'which means')?
Is there a distinctive mechanism that makes a familiar promise believable?

rubric.4: A distinctive, credible mechanism with tight cause-and-effect logic.

pos: \b(because|so that|which means|this means|that'?s why|the reason|as a result|therefore|works by|how it works|step \d|by (using|combining|automating|removing|replacing))\b

dimensions.name: Structure and flow
dimensions.description: The argument is ordered so each point earns the next: clear opening, logical sequence, signposting, a conclusion. Aristotle's arrangement (taxis).
judge_asks: Is there a clear main point up front?
Does each section follow logically from the last?
Can a skim reader get the argument from headings and first lines?

rubric.4: Tight, skimmable structure where every part earns the next.

dimensions.name: Contrast and alternatives
dimensions.description: Positions the claim against what the reader would otherwise do, including nothing. Value is judged relatively (Dunford's competitive alternatives, anchoring, before/after).
judge_asks: Does the text compare with the reader's alternatives, including the status quo?
Is there a before/after or old way/new way contrast?
Are anchors and reference points used fairly?

rubric.4: Sharp, fair contrast that makes the difference obvious.

pos: \b(compared (to|with)|versus|vs\.?|unlike|instead of|rather than|alternatives?|whereas|the old way|used to|before .{1,40} after|than (most|other|traditional))\b

dimensions.name: Objection handling
dimensions.description: Anticipates and answers the reader's doubts: price, risk, fit, effort, 'what if it doesn't work'. Two-sided arguments with refutation inoculate against later counter-arguments.
judge_asks: Which obvious objections does a sceptical reader have?
Are they raised and answered?
Is uncertainty reduced (process, guarantee, proof)?

rubric.4: Anticipates the sceptic's best objections and answers them convincingly.

pos: \b(you might (think|wonder|ask|be wondering)|but what if|what about|the catch|common questions?|faq|concerns?|objections?|even if|worried that|doesn'?t (that|this) mean)\b

dimensions.name: Clarity and cognitive ease
dimensions.description: Easy to process: plain words, short sentences, low jargon. Fluent text is judged more true and more credible; complexity triggers the croc brain filter.
judge_asks: Could the target reader understand this on one read?
Are sentences and words as short as they can be?
Is jargon used only where the audience expects it?

rubric.4: Effortless; every sentence lands first time.

dimensions.name: Fit to the moment
dimensions.description: Connects the message to what is happening now in the reader's world: a shift, a trigger, a season, a decision point. Answers 'why now?' before the reader asks.
judge_asks: Is there a clear 'why now'?
Is it tied to something current and real in the reader's world?
Does it fit where the reader is in their journey?

rubric.0: Timeless; could have been sent any year.
rubric.3: Clear, specific reason this matters now.
rubric.4: Anchored in a real, recognisable shift so the timing feels obvious.

neg: \b(in today'?s (fast-paced|ever-changing|rapidly changing) world|now more than ever)\b

dimensions.name: Cost of delay
dimensions.description: Shows what waiting costs and why the status quo is not safe. Truthful stakes, not loss framing for its own sake: gain and loss frames persuade about equally on average.
judge_asks: Is the cost of doing nothing clear?
Is it specific to this reader?
Is it truthful and proportionate?

rubric.4: Quantified, reader-specific stakes that make the status quo feel risky, without exaggeration.

positive_signals: Quantified cost per week or month
negative_signals: Stakes that serve only the speaker

pos: \b(cost of (doing nothing|inaction|waiting|delay)|every (day|week|month|quarter) (you|we|that)|falling behind|losing|the longer|status quo|if we (wait|do nothing)|before it'?s too late)\b

dimensions.name: Hope and agency
dimensions.description: Pairs urgency with optimism and a feasible path, so the reader feels able to act. Fear and urgency persuade more when efficacy is clear; urgency plus pessimism produces paralysis.
judge_asks: Does the reader feel able to act?
Is the path concrete and achievable?
Is the tone hopeful rather than doom-laden?

rubric.3: Clear, achievable path with an optimistic tone.
rubric.4: Urgency and optimism in balance: the reader feels the stakes and believes they can win.

negative_signals: Overwhelming scale with no first step

pos: \b(we can|you can|it'?s possible|here'?s how|the good news|already (working|done|proven)|in (just )?\d+ (steps|days|weeks|minutes)|first step|start (with|by)|achievable|together we)\b
\b(payback|scheduled|support package|named contact|your manager will|has already|have already|we'?ve done|hard things before|one hour)\b

dimensions.name: Genuine, shared urgency
dimensions.description: Urgency that is real and in the reader's interest, not just the speaker's. Real deadlines and capacity limits, no countdown theatre.
judge_asks: Is any deadline or scarcity real and specific?
Whose interest does the urgency serve?
Would the reader still feel fairly treated if they knew everything?

rubric.3: Real, specific urgency in the reader's interest.
rubric.4: Transparent, shared urgency the reader would endorse with full information.

positive_signals: Urgency framed around the reader's goal

neg: \b(act now|last chance|hurry|don'?t miss out|limited time only|today only|while stocks? last|before it'?s gone)\b

dimensions.name: The call to act
dimensions.description: A specific, low-friction next step, placed when the case has been made, saying what happens next. The moment the urgency is converted into action.
judge_asks: Is there one clear next step?
Is it easy and proportionate to the trust built?
Is it placed at the right moment and time-bound?

rubric.2: An ask, but generic or buried.
rubric.4: One irresistible, low-friction, time-bound step with clear consequences.

negative_signals: Ask far bigger than trust built

neg: \b(let (me|us) know if you have any questions|feel free to (reach out|contact)|any questions,? (just )?(let me know|shout))\b

lenses.name: Telos
lenses.description: The end the whole piece serves: one big idea and the change it wants in the reader (think, feel, do).
lenses.why_add: A text can score well on every appeal and still be about nothing in particular.
judge_asks: Can the core idea be said in one sentence?
Is it clear what the reader should think, feel and do afterwards?
Does every section serve that one purpose?

pos: \b(in (short|summary|a nutshell)|the (point|bottom line|big idea) is|what (this|it) means|my (ask|recommendation) is|we recommend|so what)\b

lenses.name: Mythos
lenses.description: The shared narrative, worldview or myth the message draws on: mission, belief, archetype, the story of the world the reader wants to live in. Distinct from pathos/story, which is about local anecdotes.
lenses.why_add: Brands and movements persuade through a worldview the audience joins, not only through individual claims.
judge_asks: Is there a point of view or belief about how the world should be?
Does the piece invoke a bigger narrative (old way vs new way, a shift, a mission)?
Would a reader who shares the worldview feel recognised?

pos: \b(we believe|our mission|why we|purpose|vision|the future of|the old way|the new way|movement|manifesto|it'?s time (to|for)|world where)\b

lenses.name: Prepon
lenses.description: Aristotle's appropriateness (decorum): style matched to subject, audience and medium. The right register, length and format for a CV versus a landing page versus a keynote. Includes readability for the audience (e.g. Gunning Fog under 12 for executive audiences).
lenses.why_add: Persuasive techniques in the wrong register backfire: urgency in a CV, jargon in a consumer ad, jokes in a crisis statement.
judge_asks: Is the register right for this audience and medium?
Is the length and format right for the content type?
Are any techniques used that are inappropriate for this genre?

lenses.name: Dialogue
lenses.description: Whether the text treats the reader as a partner in reasoning: it acknowledges other perspectives, answers the strongest objection, and invites a response rather than demanding agreement.
lenses.why_add: Persuasion that closes down thinking may win the moment but rarely builds lasting conviction or trust.
judge_asks: Does the text acknowledge that a reasonable person might see this differently?
Does it engage the strongest counter-view, not a straw man?
Does it invite the reader to respond, test or question?

pos: \b(some (people )?(argue|think|say)|you may (disagree|see it differently)|on the other hand|to be fair|reasonable people|i could be wrong|what do you think|tell me|i'?d (love|like) to hear|push back|let me know where)\b

archetypes.name: The Auditor
archetypes.basis: High need for cognition, prevention focus
archetypes.key_question: Can I check this, and what happens if it's wrong?

archetypes.name: The Builder
archetypes.basis: Moderate need for cognition, execution focus
archetypes.style: Practical; thinks in steps and dependencies
archetypes.key_question: Who does what, by when, with what?

archetypes.name: The Pathfinder
archetypes.style: Fast; drawn to possibility and bold moves
archetypes.key_question: What becomes possible, and what would we regret not doing?

archetypes.name: The Connector
archetypes.style: Relational; listens for intent and impact on others
archetypes.key_question: How will this land with the people affected?

archetypes.name: The Sceptic
archetypes.basis: High persuasion knowledge and reactance; has heard every pitch
archetypes.values: Independence, intellectual honesty, not being sold to
archetypes.key_question: What's the catch, and why should I believe you over what I already think?

exec_roles.question: How does it fit our estate, security and roadmap?

exec_roles.name: CTO / Head of Engineering

exec_roles.name: People Director / CHRO

exec_roles.question: Is the data good enough to support this decision?

exec_roles.name: Strategy Director

exec_roles.name: Sales Director / CRO

exec_roles.name: Sustainability Director

exec_roles.name: Procurement Lead
exec_roles.question: Is this the best value, and how do I compare it fairly?

exec_roles.name: Non-executive / Board member

perspectives.name: Classical rhetoric
perspectives.question: Is the argument well made and well said?

levers.name: Rule of three
levers.look_for: Parallel groups of three words or phrases.
levers.misuse: Empty triads that sound good but say nothing.

levers.name: Repetition and anaphora
levers.look_for: A word or phrase repeated at the start of successive clauses.
levers.misuse: Repetition used to make a weak claim feel true.

levers.name: Contrast and antithesis
levers.look_for: 'Not X, but Y'; opposites side by side.

levers.name: Rhetorical questions
levers.look_for: Questions that make the reader supply the answer.

levers.name: Brevity
levers.look_for: Short sentences and economy of words.

levers.name: Levity
levers.look_for: Lightness and wit appropriate to the setting.

perspectives.name: Social influence
perspectives.question: Which of the principles of influence are at work, and are they used truthfully?

levers.name: Reciprocity
levers.look_for: Value given first (insight, free resource, help).
levers.ethical_use: Give genuinely useful value with no strings.
levers.misuse: Token gifts used to create obligation.

levers.name: Commitment and consistency
levers.look_for: Small first steps; linking the ask to the reader's stated goals.
levers.ethical_use: Ask for steps consistent with what the reader already wants.

levers.name: Social proof
levers.look_for: What similar others do; testimonials, numbers of customers.
levers.ethical_use: Real, relevant proof from people like the reader.
levers.misuse: Fabricated or inflated numbers; norms that publicise bad behaviour.

levers.name: Authority
levers.look_for: Credentials, expertise, expert endorsement.

levers.name: Liking
levers.look_for: Similarity, compliments, cooperation, warmth.

levers.name: Scarcity
levers.look_for: Limited availability or time.

levers.name: Unity
levers.look_for: Shared identity: 'we', family, place, tribe.
quick: \b(we all|together|our community|one of us|people like us|fellow)\b

levers.name: Pre-suasion
levers.look_for: What the opening directs attention to before the ask.
levers.ethical_use: Open on what genuinely matters to the reader.

perspectives.name: Tribes and change
perspectives.question: Is it for someone specific, and does it create tension that a change resolves?

levers.name: Smallest viable audience
levers.look_for: A precise 'who it's for' (and who it isn't).
quick: \b(for (teams|founders|leaders|people|anyone) who|built for|designed for|if you'?re a|not for)\b

levers.name: People like us
levers.look_for: Norms and identity: 'people like us do things like this'.
levers.ethical_use: Invite people into a culture they want.

levers.name: Tension
levers.look_for: A gap the reader feels between now and what could be.
levers.ethical_use: Honest tension resolved by real change.
levers.misuse: Anxiety created only to sell relief.

levers.name: Status
levers.look_for: How acting changes the reader's standing (affiliation or dominance).

levers.name: Remarkability
levers.look_for: Something worth remarking on: distinctive, not just 'very good'.

levers.name: Permission and generosity
levers.look_for: Anticipated, personal, relevant; the text earns attention rather than interrupting.

perspectives.name: Behavioural economics
perspectives.question: How do framing, anchors and choice structure shape the decision?

levers.name: Anchoring
levers.look_for: A reference number presented before price or effort.

levers.name: Gain vs loss framing
levers.look_for: Whether outcomes are framed as gains or losses.
levers.ethical_use: Frame to fit the reader's focus, truthfully.

levers.name: Choice architecture
levers.look_for: Number and structure of options (good-better-best, defaults).

levers.name: The power of free
levers.look_for: Zero-price elements.

levers.name: Costly signalling
levers.look_for: Effort or commitment that signals seriousness (guarantees, investment, craft).

levers.name: Psycho-logical reframing
levers.look_for: Changing the meaning, not the thing (Sutherland).

perspectives.name: Behaviour design
perspectives.question: Will the reader actually be able and prompted to do the thing?

levers.name: Easy
levers.look_for: Low effort, clear steps, time stated.

levers.name: Attractive
levers.look_for: Salient, personal, rewarding.

levers.name: Social
levers.look_for: Others are doing it; commitment to others.

levers.name: Timely
levers.look_for: Prompt arrives at a moment of readiness.

levers.name: Clear prompt
levers.look_for: A specific trigger to act now.

levers.name: Motivation
levers.look_for: Why the reader would want to (pleasure, hope, belonging, avoiding pain).

perspectives.name: Processing and attention
perspectives.question: Does it work for how this reader will process it?

levers.name: Argument quality
levers.look_for: Strong, relevant arguments for careful readers.

levers.name: Peripheral cues
levers.look_for: Credibility, consensus and attractiveness cues for skimmers.

levers.name: Processing fluency
levers.look_for: Plain words, short sentences, clean layout.
levers.ethical_use: Make true things easy to grasp.
levers.misuse: Fluency used to make false claims feel true.

levers.name: Attention hook
levers.look_for: A first line that earns the next.
levers.ethical_use: Lead with what matters to the reader.

levers.name: Cognitive load
levers.look_for: One idea at a time; chunking.

perspectives.name: Narrative psychology
perspectives.question: Does a story carry the reader somewhere?

levers.name: Intention and obstacle
levers.look_for: Someone wants something badly; something formidable stands in the way.

levers.name: Relatable character
levers.look_for: A protagonist the reader identifies with (ideally the reader).

levers.name: Imagery and transportation
levers.look_for: Vivid scenes that let the reader enter the story.

levers.name: Shape
levers.look_for: What is vs what could be; excite, disturb, assure; three acts.

levers.name: Turning point and surprise
levers.look_for: A moment where things change unexpectedly.

levers.name: Promise and pace
levers.look_for: Early signal of where the piece is heading, a reason to keep reading, and a tight focus.
levers.misuse: Promises the piece never pays off.

levers.name: Transformation
levers.look_for: The hero ends changed; the reader sees their own change.

perspectives.name: Identity and values
perspectives.question: Whose values and identity does the message speak to?

levers.name: Values match
levers.look_for: The case is made in the audience's values, not the speaker's.

levers.name: Identity-consistent action
levers.look_for: Acting is framed as being true to who the reader is.

levers.name: Affirm before challenging
levers.look_for: Acknowledge what the reader got right before asking for change.

levers.name: No status threat
levers.look_for: The reader's past choices aren't made to look foolish.

levers.name: Shared in-group
levers.look_for: 'We' that includes the reader.

perspectives.name: Resistance and reactance
perspectives.school: Brehm, Knowles & Linn, Friestad & Wright, Berger, Sherif
perspectives.question: What will make the reader push back, and does the text reduce it?

levers.name: Freedom-preserving language
levers.look_for: Choice language rather than commands.
quick: \b(if (it'?s|that'?s) useful|your call|up to you|no pressure|if you'?d like|feel free)\b

levers.name: Objections raised and answered
levers.look_for: Counter-arguments raised then refuted.

levers.name: Low tactic visibility
levers.look_for: Persuasion that doesn't feel like a formula (no stacked hype or pressure).

levers.name: Ask within reach
levers.look_for: The step asked for is one the reader could accept today.

levers.name: Uncertainty reduced
levers.look_for: Process, guarantees, trials, proof that lower risk.

levers.name: Status quo addressed
levers.look_for: Acknowledges what the reader would give up and why it's worth it.

perspectives.name: Trust and relationship
perspectives.question: Does the reader trust the intent as well as the competence?

levers.name: Warmth before competence
levers.look_for: Signals of good intent before credentials.

levers.name: Credibility
levers.look_for: Expertise shown, not claimed.

levers.name: Reliability
levers.look_for: Commitments and track record of doing what was said.

levers.name: Intimacy
levers.look_for: Candour; safe to share concerns.

levers.name: Low self-orientation
levers.look_for: Focus on the reader, not the speaker's agenda.

levers.name: Labelling feelings
levers.look_for: Naming the reader's likely feelings.
quick: \b(it (can|may) feel|you might feel|it sounds like|it seems like)\b

perspectives.name: Motivation and emotion
perspectives.question: Does the emotional register fit the reader and lead to action?

levers.name: Regulatory fit
levers.look_for: Framing matches the reader's growth or safety focus.
levers.ethical_use: Fit the frame to the reader.

levers.name: Threat with efficacy
levers.look_for: Any threat paired with a doable response.

levers.name: Grounded optimism
levers.look_for: Hope and possibility as well as threat.

levers.name: Autonomy and mastery
levers.look_for: Appeals to growth, competence and choice.

levers.name: Emotional range
levers.look_for: Movement between emotions (concern to hope), not one note.

perspectives.name: Ethics and respect
perspectives.school: Baker & Martinson (TARES), dark-pattern research, Aristotle on eudaimonia
perspectives.question: Would the reader still feel fairly treated if they saw everything?

levers.name: Truthfulness
levers.look_for: Claims are accurate and not misleading by omission.

levers.name: Authenticity
levers.look_for: The persuader believes what they say and is who they say they are.

levers.name: Respect
levers.look_for: Treats the reader as a capable adult; no shaming or exploiting fears.

levers.name: Equity
levers.look_for: Fair to readers with less knowledge or power.

levers.name: Social responsibility
levers.look_for: Good for the wider community, not just the transaction.

levers.name: Serves flourishing
levers.look_for: Leaves the reader better off in the long run (eudaimonia), not just converted.
levers.misuse: Short-term wins that cost the reader later.

perspectives.name: Critical suspicion
perspectives.question: Who benefits from this belief, and is the reader being helped to think or just to agree?

levers.name: Who benefits
levers.look_for: The persuader's interest is visible or declared.
levers.misuse: Hidden interests dressed as neutral advice.

levers.name: Tests rather than flatters
levers.look_for: The text challenges what the reader already believes, rather than only confirming it.
levers.misuse: Telling people what they want to hear.

levers.name: Faces the strongest counter-case
levers.look_for: Engages the best argument against, not a weak version.

levers.name: Revisable conviction
levers.look_for: Says what would change the author's mind.
quick: \b(i could be wrong|if (i'?m|we'?re) wrong|would change (my|our) mind|we'?ll (stop|reconsider) if)\b

levers.name: Honest motives
levers.look_for: The real reason for the ask matches the stated reason.
levers.ethical_use: Say why you are really asking.

levers.name: Courage to reconsider
levers.look_for: Invites the reader to question a cherished assumption, without contempt.
levers.ethical_use: Help people revise beliefs with dignity.
levers.misuse: Contempt for the reader's current view.

moves.name: Turn duties into achievements
moves.how: Replace what you were responsible for with what changed because of you: action verb, what you did, measurable result.

example.before: Responsible for managing the engineering team.
example.after: Grew the engineering team from 6 to 25 and cut release time from monthly to daily.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Show judgement through diagnosis
moves.how: Demonstrate expertise by describing the reader's problem better than they can, including a cause they may not have considered.

example.before: We are experts in pricing.
example.after: Most consultancies under-price because they quote on hours. The fix is not a higher rate; it is pricing the outcome.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Make credentials relevant
moves.how: Only cite credentials this reader values, and say why they matter for the reader's problem.

example.before: MBA, PRINCE2, ITIL, Six Sigma.
example.after: Six Sigma trained, which is why our first step is always measuring your defect rate.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Swap superlatives for specifics
moves.how: Delete self-awarded praise (world-class, revolutionary) and replace it with the fact that would have earned it.

example.before: Our world-class support team is second to none.
example.after: A named engineer answers within 2 hours, 24/7.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Admit a limit, then answer it
moves.how: State one honest limitation or who this is not for, then say why it doesn't matter for this reader or how you handle it. Raising a weakness without answering it makes a message less persuasive.

example.before: Perfect for every business.
example.after: Built for teams of 10 to 200. Smaller teams can start on the free tier and move up when they need to.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Share the risk
moves.how: Offer a guarantee or commitment you can honour, so the reader is not carrying all the risk.

example.before: Contact us to get started.
example.after: If you do not see a measurable improvement in 60 days, we refund the fee.

moves.guardrail: Only offer guarantees the business will actually honour.

moves.name: Flip 'we' to 'you'
moves.how: Rewrite sentences that start with the author so they start with the reader and what they get.

example.before: We offer a comprehensive onboarding programme.
example.after: You will be up and running in your first week, with a guide on call.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Make the reader the hero
moves.how: Cast the reader as the protagonist with the goal; position the author as the guide with empathy, authority and a plan.

example.before: Our company was founded in 2009 and has grown to 200 staff.
example.after: You want a team that ships without burning out. We have helped 40 teams do exactly that, in three steps.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Give value before the ask
moves.how: Include one genuinely useful insight, tip or resource before any request.

example.before: Book a call to learn more.
example.after: Quick check you can do today: compare your last 10 lost deals against the reason given. Most turn out to be 'no decision', not price. If that is you, a call might help.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Make proof specific
moves.how: Replace vague praise with a named source, their role and the outcome they got.

example.before: "Great service, highly recommend!"
example.after: "We cut month-end close from 9 days to 3." Priya Shah, Finance Director, Northwind Logistics

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Use proof from people like the reader
moves.how: Choose testimonials and examples from the reader's own sector, size and role. Social proof works best from similar others.

example.before: Trusted by Fortune 500 companies.
example.after: Used by 120 independent accountancy practices across the UK.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Show you have been there
moves.how: Briefly share an experience that puts the author in the reader's shoes.

example.before: We help founders raise capital.
example.after: I pitched 41 investors before my first yes. Here is what I wish I had known.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Use the reader's words
moves.how: Replace the author's internal jargon with the phrases the reader uses to describe their own problem.

example.before: Our platform optimises omnichannel attribution.
example.after: See which of your ads actually led to a sale.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Clean up and stay consistent
moves.how: Fix errors and placeholders, remove shouting (caps, !!!), and hold one register throughout.

example.before: AMAZING results!!! Contact us TODAY
example.after: Clients typically see results within a month. Get in touch when you are ready.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Name the struggling moment
moves.how: Describe the specific moment the reader realises the current way is not working, in their words.

example.before: Accounting software for small businesses.
example.after: It is 11pm on the last day of the quarter and you are still matching receipts to bank lines.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Paint the dream outcome
moves.how: State the result the reader actually wants, not the deliverable.

example.before: Monthly bookkeeping.
example.after: Books done and tax-ready every month without you touching a receipt.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Feature, so what, outcome
moves.how: For each feature ask 'so what?' until you reach a benefit the reader feels.

example.before: 256-bit encryption.
example.after: Bank-grade encryption, so a lost laptop never becomes a data breach letter to your clients.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Make abstractions concrete
moves.how: Swap each abstract noun for something the reader can picture: a person, a moment, an object, a number.

example.before: We deliver holistic, seamless solutions that empower teams.
example.after: Your team sees every open ticket on one screen, so nobody chases updates in Slack.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Open with a scene
moves.how: Start with a short, specific scene before the point.

example.before: Many managers struggle with feedback.
example.after: Friday, 4.45pm. You have one review left to write and no idea how to say it.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Add a micro-story
moves.how: Insert a three-sentence story: who, what went wrong, what changed. Put it where the claim needs most belief.

example.before: Our method improves retention.
example.after: Sam ran a gym losing 30 members a month. We changed one thing: a call on day 7. Churn halved by spring.

moves.guardrail: Pair the story with the evidence behind it. The 'one story beats a statistic' effect is small; the best texts use both.

moves.name: Use STAR / CAR for examples
moves.how: Frame examples as Situation, Task, Action, Result so the reader sees the stakes and the payoff.

example.before: Worked on the payments migration.
example.after: Payments outages were costing £40k a month (S). I led the migration (T), moved us to idempotent queues (A) and we have had zero outages since (R).

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Frame action as identity
moves.how: Connect acting with who the reader is or aspires to be.

example.before: Sign up for our newsletter.
example.after: Join 4,000 engineering leaders who get one practical idea every Tuesday.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Don't make the reader wrong
moves.how: Reframe criticism of the reader's current choice so it was sensible then and the change is smart now.

example.before: If you are still using spreadsheets, you are doing it wrong.
example.after: Spreadsheets got you this far. At your size, they start costing more than they save.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Quantify the cost of doing nothing
moves.how: Show what staying put costs per week, month or year, using the reader's numbers where possible.

example.before: Don't wait to fix your hiring process.
example.after: Each month a senior role stays open costs roughly [£X] in delayed delivery.

moves.guardrail: State stakes truthfully and in the reader's terms. Don't switch to loss framing for its own sake; gain and loss frames are about equally persuasive on average.

moves.name: Give a real reason to act now
moves.how: Tie timing to something true: a deadline, a capacity limit, a season, a market shift. Delete fake urgency.

example.before: Act now! Limited time only!
example.after: We take four new clients per quarter. Two Q1 places remain.

moves.guardrail: Scarcity and deadlines must be real. Manufactured urgency fails the TARES test.

moves.name: Label the feeling
moves.how: Name what the reader is probably feeling, tentatively ('It can feel like...').

example.before: Our software handles compliance.
example.after: It can feel like every audit is a fresh scramble. It does not have to be.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Say their doubt first
moves.how: Voice the negative thing the reader is probably thinking before they do.

example.before: We are the right partner for you.
example.after: You are probably thinking: another agency promising the world. Fair. Here is what we will not promise.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Quantify the claim
moves.how: Replace every 'improved', 'faster', 'more' with a number, a time frame and a baseline.

example.before: Significantly improved performance.
example.after: Cut page load from 4.1s to 1.3s in six weeks.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Cite the source
moves.how: Attribute data and claims to a named source the reader can check.

example.before: Studies show most projects fail.
example.after: In Gartner's research, most B2B buying groups report the purchase was harder than expected.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Remove weasel words
moves.how: Delete or replace 'up to', 'many', 'significant', 'leading'. If you cannot be specific, reconsider the claim.

example.before: Save up to 50% on costs.
example.after: Customers save a median of 22% in year one.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Add the reason why
moves.how: After each claim, add 'because...' or 'which means...'.

example.before: Our coffee tastes better.
example.after: Our coffee tastes better because we roast to order and ship within 48 hours.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Name the mechanism
moves.how: Give the distinctive 'how' a name and a one-line explanation, so a familiar promise becomes newly believable.

example.before: Lose weight fast.
example.after: The 3-plate method: you change what goes on the plate, not how much.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Lead with the point
moves.how: Put the main claim or outcome in the first line. Build the case after.

example.before: Founded in 2010, we have worked across many sectors... (point in paragraph 4)
example.after: We cut onboarding time in half for B2B SaaS teams. Here is how.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Signpost and chunk
moves.how: Break the argument into labelled chunks (three reasons, two steps) with headings a skim reader can follow.

example.before: A long paragraph mixing problem, features, pricing and contact.
example.after: The problem. How it works (3 steps). What it costs. Next step.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Contrast with the status quo
moves.how: Compare with what the reader would do without you, including doing nothing, not just competitors.

example.before: Our tool tracks expenses.
example.after: Instead of a shared spreadsheet that nobody updates, expenses are logged the moment a card is used.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Show before and after
moves.how: State the before state, the after state, and the bridge between them.

example.before: We improve team productivity.
example.after: Before: 3 days to ship a fix. After: 3 hours. The bridge: automated tests on every change.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Raise and answer the objection
moves.how: Name the sceptic's strongest objection and answer it with evidence. Two-sided beats one-sided for sceptical readers.

example.before: (Price not mentioned)
example.after: Yes, we cost more than a freelancer. You are paying for a team that does not disappear in August.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Reduce uncertainty
moves.how: Explain exactly what happens next, how long it takes and what it costs, so the decision feels safe.

example.before: Get in touch for a quote.
example.after: Book a 20-minute call. You will get a fixed quote within 2 working days. No obligation.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Shorten sentences
moves.how: Split any sentence over 25 words. One idea per sentence.

example.before: Our platform, which was designed by experts with decades of experience across multiple industries, enables organisations to streamline processes while also reducing costs.
example.after: Experts designed it. It streamlines your processes. It cuts your costs.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Use plain words
moves.how: Replace long or Latinate words with short ones: use not utilise, help not facilitate, start not commence.

example.before: We facilitate the optimisation of utilisation.
example.after: We help you use what you already have.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: One clear next step
moves.how: End with a single, specific, low-friction action and say what happens when the reader takes it.

example.before: Let us know if you have any questions.
example.after: Reply 'yes' and I will send two times for a 20-minute call next week.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Anchor in this moment
moves.how: Connect the message to a current shift, event or season the reader recognises.

example.before: AI can help your team.
example.after: Since your competitors started shipping AI features this year, buyers now expect them in every demo.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Tell the bigger story
moves.how: Frame the message inside a bigger narrative: an old world, a shift, winners and losers, a promised land.

example.before: We sell sales software.
example.after: Buyers now do 70% of their research before talking to sales. The teams winning have stopped pitching and started teaching.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Pair urgency with hope
moves.how: After stating the stakes, show it can be done: a proof point, a first step, a reason for optimism. Urgency plus optimism moves people; urgency alone overwhelms them.

example.before: Cyber attacks on firms like yours rose sharply last year. You are exposed.
example.after: Attacks on firms like yours are rising. The good news: three changes block most of them, and you can make the first one this week.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Make the ask easy
moves.how: Shrink the first step until it is effortless: fewer clicks, less time, no commitment. Say exactly how long it takes.

example.before: Please complete our onboarding questionnaire.
example.after: Reply with your three biggest priorities. Two lines is fine.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Add a turn
moves.how: Include one thing the reader would not predict: a counter-intuitive fact, a reversal, a reframe. Then pay it off.

example.before: Most teams want to ship faster.
example.after: The fastest teams we studied ship less code, not more. Here's why.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Open with 'What if...?'
moves.how: Start with a question that pictures a future the reader hasn't considered possible.

example.before: Our logistics platform improves delivery times.
example.after: What if every delivery arrived in the hour your customer chose?

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Write a cold open
moves.how: Make the first one or two sentences do the work: a scene, a striking fact or the big idea. Cut the throat-clearing (welcome, background, 'I hope this finds you well').

example.before: I hope this email finds you well. My name is Tom and I work at BrightPath.
example.after: Your Q3 churn report shows 40% of losses came in month one. That is fixable.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Use the rule of three
moves.how: Group key points or benefits in threes, with parallel wording. Triads are easy to remember and feel complete.

example.before: It's fast and it's flexible and it's also open.
example.after: Fast, flexible and open.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Use contrast
moves.how: Set the old and the new side by side ('not X, but Y'). Contrast clarifies without attacking anyone.

example.before: Our approach is different from other consultancies.
example.after: Most consultancies hand you a report. We hand you a working system.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Speak to their values
moves.how: Restate the case in the values this audience holds (security, fairness, tradition, growth, care), not the values that motivate you.

example.before: This policy is the right thing to do for the planet.
example.after: This policy protects the land your members farm and the businesses their children will inherit.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Leave them free to choose
moves.how: Replace commands and pressure with choice-preserving language ('if it's useful', 'your call'). Perceived freedom lowers resistance.

example.before: You must book a demo today.
example.after: If it's useful, here's a 20-minute slot this week. Your call.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Match their focus
moves.how: For growth-minded readers frame around gains and progress; for safety-minded readers (legal, finance, risk) frame around protection and avoiding mistakes.

example.before: Unlock explosive growth with our platform.
example.after: (For a General Counsel) Reduce contract risk and keep every clause auditable.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Find the one big idea
moves.how: Write the single sentence you want the reader to remember. Put it near the start, repeat it at the end, and cut anything that doesn't serve it.

example.before: (Five equal points about features, pricing, history, team and roadmap)
example.after: One idea: we halve your onboarding time. Everything else is evidence for that.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Give every number a meaning
moves.how: Translate big or abstract numbers into something the reader can picture or compare.

example.before: We process 2.4 billion transactions a year.
example.after: We process 2.4 billion transactions a year: about 76 every second.

moves.guardrail: Use only facts the author can stand behind. Where proof is missing, insert a [placeholder] rather than inventing it.

moves.name: Invite a response
moves.how: End with a genuine question or an invitation to challenge the argument. It signals confidence and respect, and turns a pitch into a conversation.

example.before: This is clearly the right approach.
example.after: That's how we see it. Where do you think it breaks down for your team?

moves.guardrail: Ask only questions you want answered.

moves.name: Say what would change your mind
moves.how: State the evidence that would make you reconsider. It shows the conviction is examined, not inherited, and makes the claim testable.

example.before: This strategy will work.
example.after: We think this will work. If churn hasn't fallen by March, we'll stop and try the alternative.

moves.guardrail: Only commit to tests you will honour.

moves.name: Declare your interest
moves.how: Say plainly what you gain if the reader agrees. Readers discount hidden interests far more than declared ones.

example.before: Independent advice: switch to Platform X.
example.after: Full disclosure: we're a Platform X partner. Here's why we'd still recommend it, and when we wouldn't.

red_flags.name: Manufactured urgency
red_flags.description: Deadlines or scarcity with no specifics, which readers increasingly read as manipulation.
red_flags.pattern: \b(act now|last chance|hurry|don'?t miss out|limited time only|today only|while stocks? last|before it'?s gone)\b

red_flags.name: Hype and superlatives
red_flags.description: Self-awarded superlatives that cost credibility with sceptical readers.

red_flags.name: Absolute promises
red_flags.description: Guarantees of outcomes nobody can guarantee. Often a legal and compliance risk too.

red_flags.name: Weasel claims
red_flags.description: Claims that sound specific but commit to nothing ('up to', 'studies show').

red_flags.name: Fear without a path
red_flags.description: Threat or doom language with no clear, achievable response. Fear works better with efficacy; without it, low-confidence readers get defensive.

red_flags.name: Buzzword cluster
red_flags.description: Several abstract buzzwords together; the reader cannot tell what is actually being offered.

red_flags.name: Making the reader wrong
red_flags.description: Language that attacks the reader's current choice, triggering defensiveness.

red_flags.name: Confirmshaming
red_flags.description: Opt-out wording that shames the reader for declining ('No thanks, I like wasting money'). A recognised dark pattern.

red_flags.name: Controlling language
red_flags.description: Commands and pressure that threaten the reader's sense of choice, which tends to trigger reactance.
red_flags.pattern: \b(you must|you need to|you have to|you should|it is (essential|imperative) that you|don'?t wait)\b

options.label: High: reads carefully, big decision
options.guidance: Central route. Argument quality decides. Weak evidence is punished, so logos carries more weight.

options.label: Medium
options.guidance: Mixed processing.

options.label: Low: skims, small decision
options.guidance: Peripheral route. Cues (credibility, social proof, emotion, simplicity) dominate. Keep logos light and fast.

options.label: Unaware of the problem
options.guidance: Lead with story, identity or the struggling moment. Product claims will be ignored.

options.label: Problem aware
options.guidance: Agitate the problem, then introduce a mechanism.

options.label: Solution aware
options.guidance: Differentiate your mechanism; contrast with alternatives.

options.label: Product aware
options.guidance: Proof, objections and offer.

options.label: Most aware
options.guidance: State the offer and the terms. Get out of the way.

options.label: Cold: they don't know you
options.guidance: Credibility and goodwill first. Ask for small things.

options.label: Warm: some familiarity
options.guidance: Build on existing trust.

options.label: Trusted relationship
options.guidance: Credibility is assumed; focus on substance.

audience_modifiers.name: Who decides
audience_modifiers.basis: Gartner B2B buying jobs; group psychology

options.label: One person
options.guidance: Personal motivation matters more.

options.label: A buying group or panel
options.guidance: Defensibility wins. Give the champion evidence they can forward, and reduce personal blame risk.

audience_modifiers.name: Audience archetype
audience_modifiers.basis: Need for cognition (Cacioppo & Petty), regulatory focus (Higgins), and persuasion knowledge and reactance (Friestad & Wright; Brehm)

options.label: General audience
options.guidance: No archetype assumed.

options.label: The Auditor: Prove it
options.guidance: High need for cognition, prevention focus. Values accuracy, defensibility, downside protection. Persuaded by sourced numbers, downside scenarios, comparison with doing nothing; put off by round numbers with no source, enthusiasm in place of evidence. Key question: Can I check this, and what happens if it's wrong?

options.label: The Builder: Show me the plan
options.guidance: Moderate need for cognition, execution focus. Values feasibility, sequencing, resourcing, ownership. Persuaded by concrete steps, named owners, realistic timelines; put off by vision with no plan, hand-waving over effort. Key question: Who does what, by when, with what?

options.label: The Pathfinder: Where could this take us?
options.guidance: Promotion focus, big-picture processing. Values growth, ambition, advantage, momentum. Persuaded by a vivid future state, a sharp insight others missed, first-mover advantage; put off by incremental framing, detail before direction. Key question: What becomes possible, and what would we regret not doing?

options.label: The Connector: Who does this help?
options.guidance: Affiliation and warmth orientation. Values people, relationships, fairness, shared purpose. Persuaded by real human stories, candour about impact, voices of those affected; put off by people treated as numbers, spin. Key question: How will this land with the people affected?

options.label: The Sceptic: Convince me I'm wrong
options.guidance: High persuasion knowledge and reactance; has heard every pitch. Values independence, intellectual honesty, not being sold to. Persuaded by objections raised and answered, admitted limits, freedom to decide; put off by hype, pressure tactics, one-sided arguments. Key question: What's the catch, and why should I believe you over what I already think?

audience_modifiers.name: Reader's motivation
audience_modifiers.basis: Regulatory focus theory (Higgins); regulatory fit meta-analysis (Motyka et al., 2014)

options.label: Not sure
options.guidance: No framing preference assumed.

options.label: Growth: wants gains and progress
options.guidance: Frame around gains, ambition and what becomes possible.

options.label: Safety: wants to avoid mistakes
options.guidance: Frame around protection, reliability and avoiding loss or error.

audience_modifiers.name: Reader's expertise in the topic
audience_modifiers.basis: Elaboration Likelihood Model; curse of knowledge

options.label: New to the topic
options.guidance: Define terms, give context, aim for a reading age around 12 to 14 (Fog 8 to 10).

options.label: Informed
options.guidance: Some shared vocabulary; explain anything specialist (Fog 10 to 12).

options.label: Expert
options.guidance: Technical terms are fine; skip basics (Fog up to 14).

balance_rules.name: Hype risk
balance_rules.message: Emotion outruns evidence. Sceptical readers will discount it. Add proof behind the strongest emotional claims.

balance_rules.name: Dry and forgettable
balance_rules.message: Strong on facts, weak on why anyone should care. Lead with the reader's stakes or a short story.

balance_rules.name: Credibility gap
balance_rules.message: Big claims from an unestablished source. Add borrowed credibility or candour before the claims.

balance_rules.name: All about the author
balance_rules.message: The text talks mostly about the author. Flip it to the reader's world.

balance_rules.name: No clear ask
balance_rules.message: Persuasive, but towards what? Add one specific next step.

balance_rules.name: Urgency without hope
balance_rules.message: The stakes are clear but the path isn't. Urgency plus optimism moves people; urgency alone overwhelms them.

balance_rules.name: Why now?
balance_rules.message: Nothing says why this matters now. Anchor it in a current shift or decision point.

craft_metrics.name: Speaking time
craft_metrics.note: At typical presentation pace, 2,000 words is roughly a 15-minute talk.

craft_metrics.name: Gunning Fog index
craft_metrics.method: 0.4 * (words per sentence + 100 * words of 3+ syllables / words)
craft_metrics.note: Gunning's guidance: above about 12, most general readers struggle on first pass.

craft_metrics.name: Passive sentences
craft_metrics.method: Share of sentences with a be-verb plus past participle

craft_metrics.name: Emotional language
craft_metrics.method: Share of words in an emotion lexicon

craft_metrics.name: Positive vs negative tone
craft_metrics.method: Positive minus negative lexicon hits, as a share

craft_metrics.name: Rhetorical devices
craft_metrics.method: Counts of tricolon, anaphora, antithesis, rhetorical questions, alliteration

craft_metrics.name: Appeal share by words
craft_metrics.method: Each sentence is assigned the appeal with the strongest signal; shares are words in sentences per appeal (a content-analysis approach used in studies of persuasive documents).

scoring.appeal_score: 100 * sum(dimension_score * dimension_weight) / (4 * sum(dimension_weight)) for the appeal's dimensions (four appeals: ethos, pathos, logos, kairos). Content-type priority dimensions get weight x1.5.
scoring.effective_weights: content_type.weights + sum(audience_modifier.weight_delta), floored at 0.05 and renormalised to sum to 1.
scoring.balance_index: 100 - 100 * 0.5 * sum(|actual_share - effective_weight|), where actual_share = appeal_score / sum(appeal_scores). 100 means the mix matches what this content type needs.
scoring.lens_score: Same 0-4 rubric as dimensions, scaled to 0-100. Lenses are reported, not included in overall_score in v1.
scoring.red_flags: Reported separately with severity. In v1 they do not reduce scores; the judge reflects them in eth_integrity and other dimensions.
scoring.perspective_score: 0-4 per influence perspective, judged on how well its levers are used (present, relevant, ethical). Reported, not part of the overall score.
scoring.interpretation: Scores are structured judgement, not predictions of persuasive effect. Meta-analyses show most message design choices have small, inconsistent effects (O'Keefe & Hoeken, 2021). Use the app to find weaknesses and options, then test with real readers.

integrity_caps.why: Manufactured urgency cannot produce strong kairos.
Misleading claims cap credibility however polished the rest is.

scoring.duty_profile: Relative emphasis on the five rhetorical duties (sums to 100). Fit = 100 - 50 * sum(|actual - target|)/100, where the target puts 40 on the archetype's primary duty, 25 on its secondary and 12 on each other duty.

research.cite: O'Keefe & Hoeken (2021). Message design choices don't make much difference to persuasiveness and can't be counted on. Frontiers in Psychology 12:664160.
research.finding: Across 1,149 studies of 30 message variations, differences between message forms are statistically real but small (median r about .10) and inconsistent across studies.
research.implication: Treat every score as directional guidance, not a prediction of outcome. Test with real audiences.

research.cite: O'Keefe & Jensen (2006, 2009). Gain-framed vs loss-framed messages: meta-analytic reviews.
research.finding: Loss-framed messages are not generally more persuasive than gain-framed ones (165 effect sizes, N=50,780), despite loss aversion in decisions.
research.implication: Do not reward loss framing for its own sake. Reward truthful stakes and regulatory fit.

research.cite: Allen (1991); O'Keefe (1999). One-sided vs two-sided messages: meta-analyses.
research.finding: Two-sided messages that raise and refute counter-arguments beat one-sided messages; two-sided messages that raise objections without refuting them do worse than one-sided.
research.implication: Admitting a limit only helps if you then answer it.

research.cite: Tannenbaum et al. (2015). Appealing to fear: a meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin 141(6).
research.finding: Fear appeals have a small positive effect (d about .29), stronger when they include efficacy statements about how to avoid the threat; little evidence of backfire overall, though critics argue low self-efficacy audiences can react defensively.
research.implication: Urgency needs a path. Pair threat with a clear, achievable action.

research.cite: van Laer et al. (2014). The extended transportation-imagery model: a meta-analysis. Journal of Consumer Research 40(5).
research.finding: Being transported into a story (empathy with characters plus vivid imagery) drives narrative persuasion; 132 effect sizes from 76 articles.
research.implication: Score stories on character, imagery and plot, not just presence of an anecdote.

research.cite: Lee & Feeley (2016) meta-analysis; Maier et al. (2023) re-analysis.
research.finding: The identifiable victim effect is small (r about .05) and may vanish after correcting for publication bias.
research.implication: 'One story beats a statistic' is a craft heuristic, not a law. Reward story plus evidence.

research.cite: Mertens et al. (2022) nudge meta-analysis; Maier et al. (2022) and Szaszi et al. (2022) re-analyses, PNAS.
research.finding: Headline nudge effects (d about .43) shrink to near zero after publication-bias correction; nudge-unit trials show far smaller effects. Defaults are the most robust exception.
research.implication: Behaviour-design levers in text (ease, prompts) are worth checking, but expect modest effects.

research.cite: Feinberg & Willer (2015, 2019). Moral reframing.
research.finding: Arguments reframed in the audience's moral values persuade more than arguments in the speaker's own values; people rarely do this spontaneously.
research.implication: Check whose values the text speaks to.

research.cite: Motyka et al. (2014). Regulatory fit: a meta-analytic synthesis. Journal of Consumer Psychology 24(3).
research.finding: Matching message framing to the reader's promotion (gains, growth) or prevention (safety, avoiding loss) orientation increases evaluation and intention.
research.implication: Framing should fit the reader's focus, which differs by role and context.

research.cite: Friestad & Wright (1994). The Persuasion Knowledge Model. Journal of Consumer Research 21(1).
research.finding: When people recognise a persuasion tactic, they use that knowledge to cope, often by resisting; disclosure and visible tactics activate counter-arguing.
research.implication: Visible, formulaic tactics cost credibility with savvy readers.

research.cite: Brehm (1966); Rains (2013) meta-analysis of reactance.
research.finding: Threats to perceived freedom (controlling language, pressure) trigger anger and counter-arguing.
research.implication: Prefer autonomy-supportive language to commands and pressure.

research.cite: Petty & Cacioppo (1986) Elaboration Likelihood Model; Chaiken (1980) Heuristic-Systematic Model.
research.finding: Motivated, able readers weigh argument quality; others rely on cues such as source credibility and consensus.
research.implication: Weight logos by reader involvement.

research.cite: Reber & Schwarz (1999); Dechêne et al. (2010) meta-analysis of the illusory truth effect.
research.finding: Easier-to-process statements feel more true; repetition increases perceived truth.
research.implication: Clarity helps persuasion, and repetition can mislead, so judge truth separately.

research.cite: Fogg (2009) Behaviour Model; Behavioural Insights Team (2014) EAST; Michie et al. (2011) COM-B.
research.finding: Behaviour happens when motivation, ability and a prompt converge; make it Easy, Attractive, Social, Timely.
research.implication: Check whether the ask is easy, prompted and timely.

research.cite: Sherif & Hovland (1961). Social judgement theory.
research.finding: Messages inside the audience's latitude of acceptance move them; asks in the latitude of rejection backfire.
research.implication: Ask for a step the reader can accept now.

research.cite: Cohen & Sherman (2014). Self-affirmation theory.
research.finding: Affirming people's values and competence reduces defensiveness to threatening information.
research.implication: Acknowledge what the reader got right before asking them to change.

research.cite: Knowles & Linn (2004). Resistance and Persuasion: alpha and omega strategies.
research.finding: Influence works either by increasing approach forces (alpha) or by reducing resistance (omega), and omega strategies are often neglected.
research.implication: Score how well the text removes reasons not to act, not only reasons to act.

research.cite: Heinrichs, J. Thank You for Arguing.
research.finding: Practical modern treatment of Aristotle's appeals, decorum and kairos.
research.implication: Source for rhetorical devices and decorum checks.

research.cite: Godin, S. (2018). This Is Marketing.
research.finding: Marketing as change for a specific smallest viable audience, using tension, status (affiliation and dominance) and 'people like us do things like this'.
research.implication: Check who the text is for and whether it uses tension and status honestly.

research.cite: Cialdini, R. (2021). Influence, New and Expanded; Pre-Suasion (2016).
research.finding: Seven principles (reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, unity) plus pre-suasion: what you focus attention on first shapes what follows.
research.implication: Detect each principle and judge whether it is used truthfully.

research.cite: Cicero, De Oratore and Orator (55-46 BC); Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria.
research.finding: The orator has three duties (officia oratoris): to teach (docere), to delight (delectare) and to move (movere). Aristotle adds the deliberative aim of advising on future action.
research.implication: Basis for the rhetorical duties profile: what job each part of the text is doing.

research.cite: Kinneavy, J. (1986). Kairos: a neglected concept in classical rhetoric; Sipiora & Baumlin (2002), Rhetoric and Kairos.
research.finding: Kairos (timeliness, fitness to the occasion) was central to Greek rhetoric and education, though under-treated in later teaching.
research.implication: Grounds kairos as a fourth appeal with its own dimensions.

research.cite: Gunning, R. (1952). The Technique of Clear Writing; Kincaid et al. (1975) readability formulas.
research.finding: The Fog index estimates years of schooling needed to read a text on first pass; text above about 12 is hard for general readers.
research.implication: Readability targets in the craft panel and the prepon lens.

research.cite: Higgins, C. & Walker, R. (2012). Ethos, logos, pathos: strategies of persuasion in social/environmental reports. Accounting Forum 36(3).
research.finding: Content analysis can code passages of real-world documents by the appeal they use, showing how organisations mix appeals.
research.implication: Method behind 'appeal share by words'.

research.cite: Cacioppo & Petty (1982). The need for cognition; Cacioppo et al. (1996) review.
research.finding: People differ stably in how much they enjoy effortful thinking; high scorers are moved by argument quality, low scorers by cues.
research.implication: One of the two axes behind the audience archetypes.

research.cite: Kunda, Z. (1990). The case for motivated reasoning. Psychological Bulletin 108(3).
research.finding: People reach the conclusions they want to reach when they can justify them; they search and weigh evidence selectively.
research.implication: Check whether a text tests the reader's beliefs or simply flatters them.

research.cite: Nietzsche, F. Beyond Good and Evil (1886); On the Genealogy of Morality (1887).
