research.finding: Beliefs and values have histories and serve interests; ask who benefits from a belief and what drives us to accept it.
research.implication: Basis for the critical-suspicion perspective: interests, motives and the courage to revise convictions.

research.cite: Plato, dialogues (e.g. Gorgias, Meno); Mercier & Sperber (2017), The Enigma of Reason.
research.finding: Reasoning works best in exchange: people evaluate arguments better in dialogue than alone, and change their minds more when they engage with objections.
research.implication: Basis for the dialogue lens: does the text invite the reader to reason with it?

research.cite: Lewis, R. D. (1996; 3rd ed. 2006). When Cultures Collide.
research.finding: Cultures blend three poles: linear-active (task, plans, directness), multi-active (people, expressiveness, flexible time) and reactive (listening, courtesy, harmony, face). Countries sit at different points on a triangle between them.
research.implication: The anchor of HowDoesThisLand's culture model: every reader culture is a blend of the three poles.

research.cite: Hofstede, G., Hofstede, G. J. & Minkov, M. (2010). Cultures and Organizations, 3rd ed. Dimension renamed 2023: Motivation towards Achievement and Success (formerly Masculinity).
research.finding: Six dimensions: power distance, individualism, motivation towards achievement and success, uncertainty avoidance, long-term orientation, indulgence. Country scores are relative and based mostly on older survey data.
research.implication: Calibrates expected formality, group framing, detail and time horizon for each reader culture.

research.cite: Meyer, E. (2014). The Culture Map.
research.finding: Eight scales for business culture, including low- vs high-context communication, direct vs indirect negative feedback, principles-first vs applications-first persuasion, and task- vs relationship-based trust.
research.implication: Informs several of HowDoesThisLand's text-level cultural scales. Country positions in HowDoesThisLand are derived independently, not taken from Meyer's charts.

research.cite: Hall, E. T. (1976). Beyond Culture.
research.finding: High-context cultures rely on shared understanding and implicit meaning; low-context cultures spell things out.
research.implication: Basis of the explicit vs implicit scale.

research.cite: Hornikx, J. & O'Keefe, D. J. (2009) meta-analysis; updated 2023, International Journal of Business Communication.
research.finding: Ads adapted to the audience's cultural values are slightly more persuasive (r about .07), mostly for individualism vs collectivism and in Asian samples; no adaptation effect in European or Latin American samples. The 2023 update calls adaptation effective but not dependable.
research.implication: Culture fit is reported as guidance with modest weight, never as a guarantee.

research.cite: Han, S. & Shavitt, S. (1994). Persuasion and culture: advertising appeals in individualistic and collectivistic societies. JESP 30.
research.finding: Individual-benefit appeals persuaded more in the US; family and group appeals persuaded more in Korea, especially for shared products.
research.implication: Basis of the individual vs group framing scale.

research.cite: Gelfand, M. et al. (2011). Differences between tight and loose cultures: a 33-nation study. Science 332.
research.finding: Cultures differ in the strength of social norms and tolerance of deviance (tight vs loose).
research.implication: Tight cultures punish breaches of form; HowDoesThisLand weights formality and convention more heavily for them.

research.cite: Nisbett, R. (2003). The Geography of Thought.
research.finding: East Asian reasoning tends to be holistic and contextual; Western reasoning more analytic and rule-based.
research.implication: Informs the principles-first vs applications-first scale and the advice to give context before conclusions for holistic readers.

research.cite: Cialdini, R. et al. (1999). Compliance with a request in two cultures. PSPB 25.
research.finding: Personal commitment drove compliance more among US students; what peers had done drove it more among Polish students.
research.implication: Social proof carries more weight for collectivist readers; personal consistency for individualist readers.

research.cite: ISO 24495-1:2023 Plain language; Coh-Metrix research on text cohesion (Graesser, McNamara et al.).
research.finding: Readers understand and act on text faster when it is structured for them, uses familiar words and links ideas explicitly.
research.implication: Basis of the craft editor's structure, clarity and cohesion checks.

limitations.title: Message tweaks have small effects
limitations.detail: Across 1,149 studies, the choice between message forms (story vs data, gain vs loss, one- vs two-sided) makes only a small and inconsistent difference. Who the audience is, what you offer and whether they trust you usually matter more than wording.
limitations.mitigation: Scores are framed as guidance. Audience settings shape every judgement. The calibration set lets you check the app against real outcomes over time.

limitations.title: Some storytelling folk wisdom doesn't replicate
limitations.detail: Popular claims such as 'loss framing beats gain framing', 'one story beats a statistic', 'emotion is 55% body language' and big nudge effects are weaker than often taught.
limitations.mitigation: The evidence register marks each lever's evidence strength, and moves were rewritten where the research disagrees (e.g. 'admit a limit, then answer it').

limitations.title: Kairos is now a fourth appeal
limitations.detail: Aristotle's Rhetoric centres on three proofs; kairos comes from the sophists and wider Greek rhetoric. Treating it as a fourth appeal follows rhetorical scholarship that restores kairos to the centre, and catches the commonest failure in business writing: no reason to act now.
limitations.mitigation: Kairos has its own judge and weight, which you can set to zero for a classical three-appeal reading.

limitations.title: It judges the text, not the speaker
limitations.detail: Aristotle's ethos is built in the speech, but real credibility also comes from prior reputation, brand and relationship. A brilliant cold email from an unknown sender still has an ethos ceiling. The relationship modifier partly compensates.
limitations.mitigation: Audience modifier 'relationship'; future: author profile input.

limitations.title: No explicit purpose or ask
limitations.detail: A text can be credible, moving and logical and still persuade no one of anything, because it never asks.
limitations.mitigation: Telos lens (one clear purpose) and the call-to-act dimension in Kairos.

limitations.title: Story is treated as a local technique
limitations.detail: Pathos covers anecdotes, but persuasion often runs on a bigger worldview the audience joins (brands, movements, category design).

limitations.title: Style fit is missing
limitations.detail: Aristotle himself added appropriateness (prepon) to style. Without it, the model may reward techniques that are wrong for the genre.
limitations.mitigation: Prepon lens plus content-type weights and watch-outs.

limitations.title: The categories overlap
limitations.detail: A testimonial is ethos (borrowed credibility), logos (evidence) and pathos (story) at once. Forcing single labels loses information.
limitations.mitigation: Highlights can carry multiple dimensions; moves list every dimension they affect.

limitations.title: More is not always better
limitations.detail: Maximising every appeal produces hype. The right mix depends on genre and reader; a CV with high pathos is a worse CV.
limitations.mitigation: Content-type target weights, balance index and balance rules.

limitations.title: Persuasive is not the same as good
limitations.detail: The appeals themselves are morally neutral. Optimised on their own, they can reward cleverness over honesty.
limitations.mitigation: Trust risks and TARES-based checks are built into every judge and every rewrite move.

limitations.title: Culturally Western and verbal
limitations.detail: The model reflects Greek rhetoric and mostly Anglo-American sales and marketing thinking. Directness, emotional display and authority work differently across cultures, and visual or spoken delivery is not assessed.
limitations.mitigation: Future: locale modifier and multimodal judges.

limitations.title: Uneven evidence base
limitations.detail: Some underlying ideas are robust (anchoring, loss aversion), some mixed (scarcity, decoy, choice overload), some practitioner lore. Scores imply more precision than the science supports.
limitations.mitigation: Every dimension links to studies with replication status; treat scores as structured judgement, not measurement.

limitations.title: Culture changes the rules
limitations.detail: Directness, use of evidence, hierarchy and emotional display vary by culture (Erin Meyer's Culture Map). A persuasive British landing page may read as pushy in Japan or vague in Germany.
limitations.mitigation: Future: a culture modifier for directness, persuading style (principles-first vs applications-first) and trust (task vs relationship).

limitations.title: Archetypes are simplifications
limitations.detail: Real readers mix styles, and the same person reads differently under time pressure or in a group. The archetypes are built from research dimensions (need for cognition, regulatory focus, resistance to persuasion), but the five types themselves are a working model, not a validated instrument.
limitations.mitigation: Use them to prompt questions about the reader, check against what you know of the actual person, and refine with real feedback.

limitations.title: Culture is not destiny
limitations.detail: Country profiles describe averages across millions of people, rest partly on decades-old survey data, and hide regional, generational and professional cultures. Adapting to cultural values gives a small, unreliable lift in experiments, and none at all in European and Latin American samples.
limitations.mitigation: Culture fit is scored separately from persuasion, nudges appeal weights only slightly, and every profile is labelled as an estimate. Writers are prompted to check against what they know of the actual reader.

frameworks.name: Awareness levels and market sophistication
frameworks.summary: Copy must match how aware the prospect is (unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, most aware) and how sophisticated the market is (how many similar claims they have already heard). You cannot create desire, only channel existing desire onto your product.

frameworks.name: Detached, curiosity-led outbound
frameworks.summary: Outbound that feels like a helpful peer rather than a salesperson: short, plain-language messages; 'poke the bear' questions that make prospects question their status quo; detachment from the outcome; and making it easy to say no.

frameworks.name: Carnegie's human relations principles
frameworks.summary: Foundational relationship principles: do not criticise, give honest appreciation, arouse an eager want in the other person, become genuinely interested in people, remember names, listen, talk in terms of the other person's interests, and let them feel the idea is theirs.

frameworks.name: The Catalyst: REDUCE barriers to change
frameworks.summary: Instead of pushing harder, remove barriers: Reactance (people resist being pushed; give choice and ask questions), Endowment (attachment to the status quo; surface its costs), Distance (asks too far from current views; start smaller), Uncertainty (lower trial risk), Corroborating evidence (multiple sources for big changes).

frameworks.name: Category design
frameworks.summary: Define and develop a new market category with a compelling point of view about a problem the market has not named, then condition the market so you are seen as the category leader.

frameworks.name: Challenger selling
frameworks.summary: CEB research clustered B2B reps into five profiles (Hard Worker, Relationship Builder, Lone Wolf, Reactive Problem Solver, Challenger); Challengers outperformed in complex sales. They teach buyers a commercial insight that reframes their business, tailor it to each stakeholder and take control of the sale with constructive tension. The follow-up research showed most of the work is equipping 'mobilisers' (Go-getters, Teachers, Skeptics) to build consensus inside the buying group.

frameworks.name: Principles of influence
frameworks.summary: Seven reliable drivers of compliance: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity and unity. Pre-suasion adds that what you focus attention on just before a request shapes the response.

frameworks.name: Classic advertising principles
frameworks.summary: Advertising is salesmanship in print: be specific, give reasons why, test everything, offer samples, and remember that the headline does most of the work. Ogilvy added research before creativity, the big idea and consistent brand image.

frameworks.name: Community-led growth
frameworks.summary: Build a community where members gain value from each other (support, learning, networking, status) and the business gains acquisition, retention, product insight and advocacy. Design around a shared identity and purpose, with clear member value before business value.

frameworks.name: STEPPS: why things catch on
frameworks.summary: Six drivers of sharing: Social currency (sharing makes people look good), Triggers (top of mind cues), Emotion (high-arousal feelings), Public (visible use), Practical value (useful information) and Stories (ideas carried inside narratives).

frameworks.name: Classic copywriting formulas
frameworks.summary: Reusable structures for persuasive writing. AIDA: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action. PAS: Problem, Agitate, Solve. BAB: Before, After, Bridge. FAB: Features, Advantages, Benefits. 4Ps: Picture, Promise, Prove, Push.

frameworks.name: Creator content system
frameworks.summary: A synthesis of contemporary creator approaches: find your content tilt (the intersection of your expertise and an underserved audience), build an audience before the product, document rather than create, produce a pillar piece and repurpose into many platform-native pieces, give value repeatedly before asking (jab, jab, jab, right hook), and turn ideas into a personal brand and products.

frameworks.name: Crisis communication (SCCT)
frameworks.summary: Match the response to how much responsibility stakeholders attribute to the organisation. Victim crises (e.g. natural disaster) need instructing and adjusting information; accidental crises need justification and some accommodation; preventable crises need full apology and corrective action. Crisis history and prior reputation intensify attributions.

frameworks.name: Crossing the Chasm
frameworks.summary: Innovators and early adopters buy for vision; the pragmatic early majority buy for proven, complete solutions and references. Cross the gap by dominating a narrow beachhead segment with a whole product, then expand to adjacent segments like bowling pins.

frameworks.name: Customer development and the Mom Test
frameworks.summary: Validate problems and demand before scaling: talk to customers about their lives, not your idea; ask about specifics in the past rather than hypotheticals; and judge success by commitment and advancement, not compliments.

frameworks.name: CV and LinkedIn as a sales document
frameworks.summary: Treat a CV, cover letter and LinkedIn profile as marketing assets for a specific buyer (the hiring manager): position yourself for a target role, lead with a value proposition, prove it with quantified achievements, mirror the buyer's language and make the next step easy.

frameworks.name: Obviously Awesome positioning
frameworks.summary: Positioning defines how a product is the best in the world at delivering value that a well-defined set of customers cares about. Work through five components in order, plus optional trends.

frameworks.name: Positioning-led sales pitch
frameworks.summary: Turn positioning into an eight-step, buyer-centred narrative in two phases. Setup: insight, alternatives, perfect world. Follow-through: introduction, differentiated value, proof, objections (optional), the ask.

frameworks.name: Earned media and media relations
frameworks.summary: Earn coverage by offering journalists and creators genuinely newsworthy stories: timeliness, conflict or tension, human interest, novelty, data, relevance and proximity. Newsjacking inserts your expert view into breaking stories quickly. Grunig's four models range from press agentry (publicity) and public information to two-way asymmetric (persuasion based on research, Bernays's tradition) and two-way symmetric (mutual understanding), the most ethical and sustainable.

frameworks.name: Elaboration Likelihood Model
frameworks.summary: People are persuaded via a central route (careful thinking about argument quality) when they are motivated and able to process, or a peripheral route (cues such as source attractiveness, number of arguments, social proof) when they are not. Central-route attitude change lasts longer and predicts behaviour better.

frameworks.name: Gap Selling
frameworks.summary: Buyers buy change. Diagnose the current state (physical environment, problems, impact, root cause, emotions), define the future state they want, and quantify the gap between them. The bigger and clearer the gap, the more value and urgency.

frameworks.name: B2B buying jobs
frameworks.summary: B2B buying groups must complete six jobs, in no fixed order and often looping back: problem identification, solution exploration, requirements building, supplier selection, validation and consensus creation. Validation and consensus run throughout. Sellers win by making these jobs easier (buyer enablement) rather than pushing stages.

frameworks.name: Godin's permission, remarkability and smallest viable market
frameworks.summary: Marketing is the generous act of helping someone solve a problem. Choose the smallest viable market, build something remarkable (worth remarking on), earn permission to deliver anticipated, personal, relevant messages, and create change through 'people like us do things like this'.

frameworks.name: Golden Circle
frameworks.summary: Communicate from the inside out: why you exist (purpose), how you do it (values, approach), then what you sell.

frameworks.name: Grand Slam Offer
frameworks.summary: A process for building an offer so differentiated that buyers cannot compare it on price: pick a starving crowd, list every obstacle, turn each into a solution, choose delivery vehicles, trim and stack, then enhance with scarcity, urgency, bonuses, guarantees and naming.

frameworks.name: Group psychology of buying
frameworks.summary: Groups decide differently from individuals. People conform to visible majorities (Asch), favour their in-group (social identity theory), suppress dissent to preserve harmony (groupthink), and in crowds can adopt simplified, emotional thinking (Le Bon, now considered dated). In buying committees, the dominant fear is personal blame for a bad choice, so safety, consensus and defensibility often beat optimal value.

frameworks.name: Four business stories
frameworks.summary: Businesses need four stories: the value story (how the product changes a customer's life), the founder story, the purpose story (what the organisation stands for, often told to employees) and the customer story told by customers. Great stories have an identifiable character, authentic emotion, a significant moment and specific details. Duarte's presentation structure alternates between 'what is' and 'what could be' before ending on a new bliss.

frameworks.name: Hook, Story, Offer and the Attractive Character
frameworks.summary: Every piece of marketing needs a hook to grab attention, a story that builds value and breaks false beliefs (the epiphany bridge), and an offer. A relatable 'attractive character' with a backstory, parables, flaws and polarity builds an audience.

frameworks.name: How Brands Grow (Ehrenberg-Bass laws)
frameworks.summary: Brands grow mainly by increasing penetration (more buyers, mostly light buyers), which requires mental availability (being thought of in buying situations) and physical availability (being easy to buy). Reach broadly, continuously, with consistent distinctive assets.

frameworks.name: STAR / CAR storytelling for interviews
frameworks.summary: Answer behavioural interview questions and write achievement bullets with a compact story: the situation and task (or challenge), the specific action you took, and the measurable result.

frameworks.name: Jobs to be Done and the Forces of Progress
frameworks.summary: People 'hire' products to make progress in a particular circumstance. Four forces govern switching: the push of the current situation, the pull of the new solution, anxiety about the new, and habit of the present.

frameworks.name: Key Person of Influence (5 Ps)
frameworks.summary: Become one of the most valued people in a micro-niche by working through five steps in order: a clear pitch, published content (ideally a book), productised offers, a strong online and offline profile, and partnerships with others who serve your audience.

frameworks.name: SUCCESs: making ideas stick
frameworks.summary: Sticky ideas are Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional and told as Stories. Beware the curse of knowledge: experts forget what it is like not to know.

frameworks.name: MEDDIC / MEDDPICC
frameworks.summary: An enterprise qualification and deal-inspection framework developed at PTC: Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Paper process, Identify (or Implicate) pain, Champion and Competition.

frameworks.name: Specific knowledge, accountability and leverage
frameworks.summary: Wealth comes from giving society what it wants but does not yet know how to get, at scale. Combine specific knowledge (hard to train, often found through curiosity), accountability (risk under your own name) and leverage (labour, capital, and permissionless leverage from code and media). Being able to both build and sell is a rare and powerful combination.

frameworks.name: Relationship networking (Givers Gain, VCP, Never Eat Alone)
frameworks.summary: Networking works when you give first, build relationships before you need them, and move people from visibility (they know of you) to credibility (they trust you) to profitability (they refer you). Stay in touch with regular, light 'pings' and be genuinely interested in others.

frameworks.name: New Sales. Simplified.
frameworks.summary: A simple new-business system: choose strategic target accounts, craft a compelling sales story and power statement (client issues addressed, offerings, differentiators), proactively prospect by phone and email, and lead discovery-driven meetings.

frameworks.name: NLP-derived rapport techniques
frameworks.summary: Techniques popularised by NLP for building rapport and clarifying meaning: match and pace posture, pace and language before leading; use the meta model to recover deleted, distorted or generalised information ('Who specifically?', 'Compared to what?'); and use vague, permissive language (Milton model) to invite rather than direct.

frameworks.name: The 1-Page Marketing Plan
frameworks.summary: A nine-square plan across three phases: before (prospects: target market, message, media), during (leads: capture, nurture, convert) and after (customers: deliver world-class experience, increase lifetime value, orchestrate referrals). Builds on Kennedy's message-market-media triangle.

frameworks.name: Oversubscribed campaign method
frameworks.summary: Build more demand than you can supply by running campaigns rather than selling continuously: know your capacity, warm up the market while collecting signals of interest, release at a defined moment, follow up with structured sales conversations, then celebrate, deliver beyond expectations and innovate.

frameworks.name: Personality and behavioural styles in selling
frameworks.summary: Style models help sellers adapt. Social Styles (Merrill and Reid) maps assertiveness and responsiveness into Driver, Expressive, Amiable and Analytical. DISC (derived from Marston) uses Dominance, Influence, Steadiness and Conscientiousness. The Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism) is the most scientifically supported model. Research by Adam Grant found ambiverts sold more than strong introverts or extroverts.

frameworks.name: PESO model
frameworks.summary: Integrate four media types: Paid (advertising, sponsored content), Earned (press coverage, reviews, mentions), Shared (social media and communities) and Owned (website, blog, newsletter). Strongest results come where they overlap, for example owned content amplified by paid and shared, generating earned coverage.

frameworks.name: Power bases and stakeholder politics
frameworks.summary: People hold power from different bases: legitimate (role), reward, coercive, expert, referent (admiration), and informational. Map stakeholders by power and interest (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor). Pfeffer argues that power comes from resources, networks, visibility and willingness to ask, and that ignoring politics is a career and deal risk.

frameworks.name: Product-led growth
frameworks.summary: Use the product itself as the main driver of acquisition, conversion and expansion: free trials, freemium or reverse trials let users reach value quickly; product usage signals (product-qualified leads) tell sales whom to help; pricing scales with value.

frameworks.name: Psycho-logic and behavioural reframing
frameworks.summary: Human decisions follow psycho-logic, not economic logic. Small changes to framing, context, signalling and perception can create more value than expensive changes to the product itself.

frameworks.name: Psychology of money and pricing
frameworks.summary: People do not treat money rationally. They keep mental accounts, feel a 'pain of paying' that varies by payment method, anchor on reference prices, overvalue free, judge quality by price, fear losses more than they value gains, and make money decisions shaped by personal history (Housel's point that everyone's behaviour makes sense to them given their experience).

frameworks.name: Positioning in the mind
frameworks.summary: Positioning is what you do to the mind of the prospect. In an over-communicated world, own a single word or idea, be first in a category or create a new one you can be first in.

frameworks.name: Diagnosis, strategy, tactics
frameworks.summary: Start with diagnosis (research the customer and market, not your own opinions), then strategy (segmentation, targeting, positioning, objectives), and only then tactics (the 4Ps and channels).

frameworks.name: Sandler Selling System
frameworks.summary: A buyer-and-seller-as-equals approach that removes pressure on both sides: build rapport, agree an up-front contract for each meeting, uncover pain, discuss budget and decision process, then present only what addresses the pain, and secure the post-sell.

frameworks.name: SPIN Selling
frameworks.summary: A questioning sequence for large, complex sales derived from research into tens of thousands of sales calls: ask a few situation questions, uncover problems, explore implications to build urgency, then ask need-payoff questions so the buyer articulates the value.

frameworks.name: StoryBrand SB7
frameworks.summary: Position the customer as the hero and the brand as the guide: a character with a problem meets a guide who gives them a plan and calls them to action, helping them avoid failure and achieve success.

frameworks.name: Strategic narrative
frameworks.summary: Structure a pitch or company story around an undeniable shift in the world: name the shift, show there will be winners and losers, tease the promised land, introduce features as 'magic gifts' that get you there, then present evidence.

frameworks.name: STRONG pitch method and frame control
frameworks.summary: Pitches are first filtered by the primitive 'croc brain', which ignores anything boring, complex or threatening. Win by controlling the frame and following STRONG: Set the frame, Tell the story, Reveal the intrigue, Offer the prize, Nail the hook point, Get a decision.

frameworks.name: Supercommunicators: matching the conversation
frameworks.summary: Conversations are of three kinds: practical ('What's this really about?'), emotional ('How do we feel?') and social ('Who are we?'). Connection comes from noticing which conversation is happening and matching it, asking deep questions, and 'looping for understanding' (ask, repeat back, check you got it right).

frameworks.name: TARES test for ethical persuasion
frameworks.summary: Five tests for persuasive communication: Truthfulness of the message, Authenticity of the persuader, Respect for the persuadee, Equity of the appeal (fair, not exploiting vulnerability or information gaps), Social responsibility for the common good.

frameworks.name: They Ask, You Answer
frameworks.summary: Become the most trusted teacher in your space by honestly answering every question buyers ask, especially the topics companies avoid: cost and price, problems, comparisons, reviews and 'best of' lists. Sales teams then use that content to educate prospects before calls.

frameworks.name: To Sell Is Human: ABCs, pitch, improvise, serve
frameworks.summary: Most people spend much of their working day 'moving others' even if they are not in sales. In a world of information parity (caveat venditor, seller beware), replace 'Always Be Closing' with Attunement, Buoyancy and Clarity, then pitch, improvise and serve.

frameworks.name: Trust Equation
frameworks.summary: Trustworthiness = (Credibility + Reliability + Intimacy) / Self-orientation. Credibility is about words, reliability about actions, intimacy about safety in sharing, and self-orientation about focus on yourself rather than the client.

frameworks.name: Value-based pricing for expertise
frameworks.summary: For services, price on the value of the outcome to the client rather than time or deliverables; have the money conversation early and offer options.

frameworks.name: Value Equation
frameworks.summary: Perceived value rises with the dream outcome and the buyer's belief they will achieve it, and falls with how long it takes and how much effort or sacrifice it demands.

frameworks.name: Value Ladder
frameworks.summary: Arrange offers from free or low-priced entry points up to high-value, high-price programmes so customers can ascend as trust and need grow.

frameworks.name: Tactical empathy negotiation
frameworks.summary: Negotiation as emotional intelligence: use tactical empathy, mirroring, labelling, accusation audits and calibrated 'how' and 'what' questions to understand the other side and let them feel in control; aim for 'that's right'; use no-oriented questions; and bargain with structured concessions.

frameworks.name: Warmth and competence
frameworks.summary: People judge others (and brands) on two dimensions: warmth (intentions: friend or foe?) and competence (ability to act on intentions). Warmth tends to be judged first. High warmth and high competence elicit admiration and cooperation.

frameworks.name: Why change, why now, why you
frameworks.summary: Buyers move through three decisions: why change (break status quo bias by exposing an unconsidered need), why now (urgency) and why you (differentiation). Different messages are needed for each; most sellers jump straight to 'why you'.

frameworks.name: Win Without Pitching
frameworks.summary: Firms selling expertise should behave like doctors, not vendors: specialise to become experts, diagnose before prescribing, refuse to give away free solutions in pitches, talk money early, and lead the client through the buying process.

frameworks.name: Working backwards (PR/FAQ)
frameworks.summary: Before building, write the press release announcing the finished product from the customer's point of view, plus an FAQ covering customer and internal questions. If the press release is not compelling, the product is not worth building.

concepts.definition: A heuristic that buyers need substantial exposure before trusting you; commonly described as around seven hours of content, eleven touchpoints and four different locations or media.

concepts.name: 95:5 rule
concepts.definition: At any time only a small share (around 5 percent per quarter) of B2B buyers are in market; most are not.

concepts.name: Accusation audit
concepts.definition: Listing the negative things the other side may think about you before they say them.

concepts.name: Anchoring
concepts.definition: The first number presented shapes judgements of what follows.

concepts.name: Attractive character
concepts.definition: A relatable public persona with backstory, parables, flaws and polarity that builds audience connection.

concepts.name: Attunement
concepts.definition: Bringing yourself into harmony with another person's perspective, interests and context.

concepts.name: Authority
concepts.definition: People defer to credible experts.

concepts.name: Awareness levels
concepts.definition: Unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, most aware.

concepts.name: The power of 'because'
concepts.definition: Giving a reason, even a weak one, increases compliance for small requests; for bigger requests the reason must be real.

concepts.name: The big idea
concepts.definition: A distinctive creative concept strong enough to anchor a campaign for years.

concepts.name: Blame avoidance
concepts.definition: In group purchases, individuals prioritise avoiding personal blame over maximising value.

concepts.name: Buying group consensus
concepts.definition: B2B purchases involve multiple stakeholders whose disagreement often leads to no decision.

concepts.name: Category creation
concepts.definition: Defining a new market category you can lead, rather than competing as one of many in an existing one.

concepts.name: Category entry points
concepts.definition: The cues (situations, needs, times, places) that prompt buyers to think of a category.

concepts.name: Central and peripheral routes
concepts.definition: Persuasion through careful evaluation of arguments versus through cues like credibility and social proof.

concepts.name: Commercial insight
concepts.definition: A reframe that teaches the buyer something new about their business, is backed by evidence and leads uniquely to your strengths.

concepts.name: Commitment and consistency
concepts.definition: After a small commitment, people act consistently with it.

concepts.name: Competitive alternatives
concepts.definition: What buyers would do if you did not exist, including doing nothing or a spreadsheet.

concepts.name: Cost of inaction
concepts.definition: The quantified consequence of doing nothing; the real competitor in most deals.

concepts.name: Costly signalling
concepts.definition: Effort and expense signal commitment and quality in ways cheap messages cannot.

concepts.name: Croc brain filtering
concepts.definition: Klaff's metaphor for fast, primitive attention filters that ignore anything boring, complex or threatening, favouring novelty and simplicity.

concepts.name: Curse of knowledge
concepts.definition: Experts cannot easily imagine not knowing what they know, so they communicate abstractly.

concepts.name: Decoy effect
concepts.definition: Adding a clearly inferior option makes a target option look better.

concepts.name: Detachment from outcome
concepts.definition: Seeking the truth about fit rather than a yes; lowers pressure and raises honesty.

concepts.name: Diagnose before you prescribe
concepts.definition: Recommending a solution before understanding the problem is malpractice, in medicine and in sales.

concepts.name: Distinctive brand assets
concepts.definition: Non-name elements such as colours, shapes, characters, sounds and phrases that trigger brand recognition.

concepts.name: Emotional intelligence
concepts.definition: Recognising and managing your own emotions and those of others.

concepts.name: Endowment effect
concepts.definition: People value what they own more than equivalent things they do not.

concepts.name: Epiphany bridge
concepts.definition: Telling the story of how you discovered a new opportunity so the audience experiences the same realisation.

concepts.name: Expert versus vendor
concepts.definition: Experts are sought out, diagnose and set terms; vendors respond to requests and compete on price.

concepts.name: Foot in the door
concepts.definition: Agreeing to a small request increases the likelihood of agreeing to a larger one later.

concepts.name: Four cores of credibility
concepts.definition: Integrity, intent, capabilities and results underpin trust.

concepts.name: Framing effect
concepts.definition: Logically equivalent options are chosen differently depending on whether they are framed as gains or losses.

concepts.name: The gap
concepts.definition: The difference between a buyer's current state and desired future state; the size of the gap sets value and urgency.

concepts.name: Givers gain
concepts.definition: Helping others succeed builds reciprocal goodwill and referrals.

concepts.name: Halo effect
concepts.definition: A positive impression in one area spills over into judgements of other areas.

concepts.name: Customer as hero, brand as guide
concepts.definition: The customer drives the story; the brand provides empathy, authority and a plan.

concepts.name: Influence versus manipulation
concepts.definition: Influence helps people make choices they would endorse with full information; manipulation bypasses or exploits their judgement.

concepts.name: Inoculation
concepts.definition: Exposing people to weakened counter-arguments and refuting them builds resistance to later persuasion.

concepts.name: Jab, jab, jab, right hook
concepts.definition: Give value repeatedly (jabs) before making an ask (right hook), in platform-native formats.

concepts.name: Labelling
concepts.definition: Naming an emotion or dynamic ('It sounds like…') to defuse negatives and reinforce positives.

concepts.name: Liking
concepts.definition: People say yes to those they like: similarity, compliments, cooperation.

concepts.name: Loss aversion
concepts.definition: Losses are felt more strongly than equivalent gains.

concepts.name: Market sophistication
concepts.definition: How many similar claims a market has heard; determines whether to lead with a claim, a bigger claim, a mechanism or identification.

concepts.name: Mass desire
concepts.definition: Copy channels existing, widely shared desires rather than creating new ones.

concepts.name: Matching and pacing
concepts.definition: Subtly matching another person's pace, energy and language before leading them somewhere new.

concepts.name: Mental accounting
concepts.definition: People categorise money into separate accounts and treat it differently.

concepts.name: Newsjacking
concepts.definition: Adding your credible perspective to a breaking news story while journalists are still seeking angles.

concepts.name: No decision is the main competitor
concepts.definition: Many deals are lost to the status quo rather than to rivals, driven by fear of making the wrong choice.

concepts.name: Sell the outcome, not the product
concepts.definition: Buyers want results; the product is just the means.

concepts.name: Pain funnel
concepts.definition: A sequence of questions moving from surface problem to business impact to personal impact.

concepts.name: Peak-end rule
concepts.definition: People judge experiences largely by their most intense moment and how they end.

concepts.name: People like us do things like this
concepts.definition: Behaviour change spreads through cultural norms and identity within a group.

concepts.name: Permission marketing
concepts.definition: The privilege of delivering anticipated, personal and relevant messages to people who want them.

concepts.name: Positioning in the mind
concepts.definition: Positioning is the place your brand occupies in the prospect's mind relative to alternatives.

concepts.name: The power of free
concepts.definition: A zero price creates disproportionate demand compared with a very low price.

concepts.name: Pratfall effect
concepts.definition: A competent person who shows a small, honest flaw can become more likeable.

concepts.name: Strategy of preeminence
concepts.definition: Act as the client's most trusted adviser, putting their interests first, even recommending others when better.

concepts.name: Pre-suasion
concepts.definition: What you direct attention to before a request changes how it is received.

concepts.name: Reactance
concepts.definition: When people feel their freedom is threatened, they resist the push.

concepts.name: Reciprocity
concepts.definition: People feel obliged to return favours.

concepts.name: Remarkability (purple cow)
concepts.definition: Products worth remarking on spread themselves; very good is now invisible.

concepts.name: Risk reversal and guarantees
concepts.definition: Shifting the risk of a bad outcome from buyer to seller via guarantees (unconditional, conditional, performance-based or anti-guarantees).

concepts.name: Scarcity and urgency
concepts.definition: People value what is limited or time-bound. Ethical only when real (capacity, cohort dates, price changes).

concepts.name: Self-orientation
concepts.definition: Focus on yourself (quota, ego, appearing clever) rather than the client; the main destroyer of trust.

concepts.name: Ask for the signal, not the sale
concepts.definition: Collect low-commitment indications of interest (waitlists, quiz completions, event sign-ups) before opening sales.

concepts.name: Smallest viable market
concepts.definition: The minimum audience you need to serve to make the work sustainable; focus there first.

concepts.name: Social currency
concepts.definition: People share things that make them look good, smart or in the know.

concepts.name: Social identity
concepts.definition: People define themselves partly by group memberships and adopt group norms.

concepts.name: Descriptive social norms
concepts.definition: Telling people what similar others do changes behaviour, especially when the reference group is close to them.

concepts.name: Social proof
concepts.definition: People look to similar others to decide what to do.

concepts.name: Specific knowledge
concepts.definition: Knowledge that cannot easily be taught, found through genuine curiosity, and often a unique combination of skills.

concepts.name: Specificity and testing
concepts.definition: Specific claims are more believable; measured tests should settle creative debates.

concepts.name: Status
concepts.definition: Perceived social standing shapes how messages are received; buyers and cultures are organised around status roles.

concepts.name: Status threat
concepts.definition: Proposals that make a stakeholder look wrong or less important trigger resistance regardless of merit.

concepts.name: Struggling moment
concepts.definition: The circumstance in which someone realises the current way is no longer good enough and begins looking for progress.

concepts.name: System 1 and System 2
concepts.definition: Fast, intuitive thinking versus slow, deliberate thinking; most buying runs on System 1.

concepts.name: Tactical empathy
concepts.definition: Understanding and articulating the other side's feelings and perspective to influence them.

concepts.name: Thin slicing and first impressions
concepts.definition: People form fast, fairly consistent judgements from brief exposures.

concepts.name: Three kinds of conversation
concepts.definition: Practical, emotional and social conversations need different responses.

concepts.name: Time to value
concepts.definition: How quickly a new customer experiences meaningful benefit.

concepts.name: Unique mechanism
concepts.definition: The distinctive 'how' behind a result that makes a familiar promise newly believable.

concepts.name: Unity
concepts.definition: Shared identity creates strong influence.

concepts.name: Visibility, credibility, profitability
concepts.definition: Relationships progress from being known, to being trusted, to generating referrals.

concepts.name: Versatility
concepts.definition: Willingness and ability to adapt your style to others; more predictive of effectiveness than your own style.

concepts.name: Warmth before competence
concepts.definition: People judge intent (warmth) before ability (competence); warmth sets the frame for how competence is received.

thinkers.name: Gartner B2B buying research (Brent Adamson and colleagues)
David Maister, Charles H. Green and Robert Galford

studies.name: Anchoring and adjustment
studies.finding: Estimates were biased towards arbitrary initial numbers (e.g. from a spun wheel).

studies.name: Asch conformity experiments
studies.finding: Participants judging line lengths frequently conformed to a unanimous but wrong majority of confederates; a single dissenting ally sharply reduced conformity.

studies.name: The copy machine study ('because')
studies.finding: People allowed someone to jump a photocopier queue more often when a reason was given, even a vacuous one, for small requests; for larger requests a real reason mattered.

studies.name: Asymmetric dominance (decoy effect)
studies.finding: Adding an option clearly inferior to one alternative increased that alternative's choice share.

studies.name: ELM exam policy study
studies.finding: When an exam policy affected students personally, argument quality drove attitudes; when it did not, source expertise mattered more.

studies.name: Endowment effect (mugs)
studies.finding: People given a mug demanded roughly twice as much to sell it as others would pay to buy it.

studies.name: Foot-in-the-door
studies.finding: Homeowners who first agreed to a small request (e.g. a small sign) were far more likely to later agree to a large one (a big billboard).

studies.name: Framing effect (Asian disease problem)
studies.finding: Identical outcomes framed as lives saved versus lives lost produced opposite risk preferences.

studies.name: Hotel towel reuse (social norms)
studies.finding: Messages saying most guests (especially in the same room) reused towels increased reuse more than environmental appeals.

studies.name: Inoculation theory
studies.finding: Exposure to weakened counter-arguments with refutation increased resistance to later persuasion.

studies.name: Minimal group paradigm
studies.finding: People assigned to groups on trivial criteria favoured their own group.

studies.name: Mints and tips (reciprocity)
studies.finding: Giving diners mints with the bill increased tips, especially when the gift seemed personal and unexpected.

studies.name: Peak-end rule (cold water)
studies.finding: Participants preferred a longer cold-water trial that ended slightly less painfully over a shorter one, judging by peak and end.

studies.name: Pratfall effect
studies.finding: A highly competent person who committed a minor blunder was rated more likeable; the effect reversed for average performers.

studies.name: Prospect theory and loss aversion
studies.finding: People evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point and weigh losses more heavily than equivalent gains.

studies.name: Cookie jar scarcity
studies.finding: Cookies from a jar with two cookies were rated more desirable than identical cookies from a jar of ten, especially when scarcity resulted from demand.

studies.name: Source credibility and the sleeper effect
studies.finding: High-credibility sources were initially more persuasive; over time, messages from low-credibility sources gained influence as the source was forgotten.

studies.name: Thin slices of behaviour
studies.finding: Ratings of teachers from silent clips under 30 seconds predicted end-of-term student evaluations.

studies.name: Stereotype content model studies
studies.finding: Groups are perceived along warmth and competence, producing distinct emotional reactions.

duties.name: Teach
duties.description: Facts, evidence and explanation: what is true and how it works.
duties.signals: Data, findings, definitions, 'because', 'which means', worked examples, analogies.
pos: \b(data|found|finding|survey|results?|according to|evidence|research|how (it|this) works|because|which means|this means|for example|for instance|in other words|think of it as)\b

duties.name: Delight
duties.description: Curiosity, wit, surprise, scene and voice that make the reader want to keep going.
duties.signals: Anecdote, humour, curiosity gaps, vivid scenes, rhythm.
pos: \b(funny|laugh\w*|surpris\w*|turns out|here'?s the thing|picture this|one day|believe it or not|imagine (if|a))\b

duties.name: Move
duties.description: Emotion, values, belief and identity: why it matters and why the reader should care.
duties.signals: Values, hope, purpose, belonging, 'together', the reader's stakes.

duties.name: Steer
duties.description: Aristotle's deliberative aim: options, a recommendation, a plan and the next step.
duties.signals: Recommendations, options, plans, decisions, next steps.

duties.name: Unsettle
duties.description: Socratic questioning: exposing an assumption, a myth or a blind spot so the reader reconsiders.
duties.signals: 'What if', 'most people think... but', myths, reversals, uncomfortable truths.
pos: \b(what if|myth|wrong|rethink|assum\w*|the truth is|most people think|contrary|uncomfortable|blind spot|actually)\b

brand.name: HowDoesThisLand
brand.origin: Named for the question every writer should ask before pressing send: how does this land with the person reading it? The method behind it goes back to Peitho (Πειθώ), the Greek goddess of persuasion, and to Aristotle's Rhetoric.
brand.meaning: More than convincing: winning someone over, inspiring confidence, reaching agreement and shaping how people think.
secondary_lines: Persuasion that still works when the reader can see how it's done.
brand.central_idea: Meaningful change happens when people engage with different perspectives, question their assumptions and reconsider what they believe.

principles.name: Persuasion
principles.statement: Influencing how people think through reasoned argument, dialogue and communication.
principles.in_the_model: The four appeals, thirteen influence perspectives and the rewrite moves.

principles.name: Trust
principles.statement: The confidence that lets people be open and receptive to one another.
principles.in_the_model: Ethos, the trust perspective, trust risks, and score caps that reserve the best scores for text that earns them.

principles.name: Dialogue
principles.statement: The exchange of perspectives through which people understand each other better.
principles.in_the_model: The dialogue lens, objection handling, and the 'invite a response' move.

principles.name: Reason
principles.statement: Using evidence, logic and critical thinking to examine beliefs.
principles.in_the_model: Logos, the evidence register, and a judge that must quote the text for every claim.

principles.name: Conviction
principles.statement: Beliefs that have been examined, not simply inherited or accepted.
principles.in_the_model: The unsettle duty, the critical-suspicion perspective, and 'say what would change your mind'.

glossary.where: The goddess of persuasion, and the coin on the About page.
Ethos and the trust perspective. Aristotle also used pisteis for the modes of persuasion.
Ethics perspective: does the persuasion leave the reader better off?

critical_questions.source: A Nietzschean challenge to the idea that persuasion is simply about arriving at objective truth.
questions: Who benefits from the beliefs we hold?
What motivates us to accept one argument over another?
Are we genuinely changing our minds, or simply seeking confirmation?
What would it take to have the courage to abandon a deeply held conviction?
critical_questions.in_the_model: The critical-suspicion perspective asks these of every text, and every rewrite leaves the final decision with the reader.

visual.direction: Intellectual and connected: editorial typography, clean contemporary layout, overlapping forms for perspectives meeting. Classical references used sparingly, never marble-and-columns.
visual.mark: Two overlapping circles; the shared space between them is where perspectives meet.
visual.type: Newsreader (editorial serif) for the wordmark and reading text; Schibsted Grotesk for interface.

groups.name: Craft
groups.question: Is it well made: shaped, sized, clear, connected and in the right voice?

groups.name: Audience
groups.question: Does it suit this particular reader, from the first line to the last?

groups.name: Culture
groups.question: Will it land well in the reader's culture?

extra_dimensions.name: Structure
extra_dimensions.description: The shape of the piece: the point comes early, sections build in a sensible order, and it ends with where to go next.
judge_asks: Is the main point in the first few lines?
Does each part follow from the last?
Is there a clear ending or next step?

rubric.3: Clear opening, logical order, clean ending.
rubric.4: Every section earns the next; a skim reader gets the whole argument.

extra_dimensions.advice: Put the main point or ask in the first two sentences, then order the rest as reasons, proof, next step.

example.before: We have been operating since 2010 and offer many services... (ask in the final paragraph)
example.after: We can halve your onboarding time. Here's how, and what it would take.

extra_dimensions.name: Length
extra_dimensions.description: Whether the length suits the content type and the reader's time: long enough to make the case, short enough to be read.
judge_asks: Is it the right length for this kind of text?
Is anything there that doesn't earn its place?
Is anything essential missing?

rubric.0: Wildly too long or too short.
rubric.4: Every sentence earns its place.

extra_dimensions.advice: Cut anything that doesn't serve the one big idea; aim for the usual range for this content type.

example.before: (A 600-word cold email)
example.after: (The same email at 120 words, with one ask)

extra_dimensions.name: Clarity and readability
extra_dimensions.description: How easily the intended reader can process the text: sentence length, familiar words, active voice, low jargon.
judge_asks: Could the reader follow it on one pass?
Are sentences and words as short as they can be?
Is jargon used only where the reader expects it?

rubric.4: Effortless.

extra_dimensions.advice: Split long sentences, prefer everyday words, and turn passive constructions active.

example.before: It has been determined that an optimisation of resource utilisation is required.
example.after: We need to use our people's time better.

extra_dimensions.name: Cohesion
extra_dimensions.description: How well the ideas hang together: sentences connect, links are signalled, key terms stay consistent, and paragraphs share a thread.
judge_asks: Does each sentence connect to the one before?
Are transitions signalled (because, so, however, for example)?
Do key terms stay consistent?

rubric.1: Frequent jumps; reader must infer links.
rubric.4: Seamless: one line of thought from start to finish.

extra_dimensions.advice: Link ideas explicitly with connectives, repeat key terms instead of synonyms, and start paragraphs by picking up the last thread.

example.before: Costs rose. Our team is experienced. Clients like us.
example.after: Costs rose, so clients need a partner who can deliver for less. That's where our experience helps.

extra_dimensions.name: Tone and voice
extra_dimensions.description: Whether the voice is consistent and right for the form, the relationship and the reader's culture: formality, warmth, confidence.
judge_asks: Is the tone consistent from start to finish?
Is the formality right for this reader and relationship?
Does it sound confident without arrogance?

rubric.4: A distinctive, well-pitched voice the reader warms to.

extra_dimensions.advice: Pick one register for this reader and hold it; remove exclamation marks and hedges that undercut it.

example.before: Hey!! Super excited to share our awesome proposal... We respectfully submit the following.
example.after: Thank you for the chance to propose. Here is what we suggest and why.

extra_dimensions.name: Claims you can stand behind
extra_dimensions.description: Whether every claim could be backed up if the reader asked: sources for statistics, evidence for comparisons, no promises the writer can't keep.
judge_asks: Could each factual claim be supported if challenged?
Are statistics sourced?
Are comparisons and guarantees defensible?

rubric.0: Several claims that couldn't be defended.
rubric.2: Mostly defensible, a few loose claims.
rubric.4: Every claim is sourced or self-evidently true.

extra_dimensions.advice: Source each statistic, soften or cut claims you can't prove, and make comparisons specific and fair.

example.before: We're the UK's leading provider, proven to double sales.
example.after: Our 140 clients grew sales by a median of 18% in year one (2025 client survey).

extra_dimensions.name: Fit to this reader
extra_dimensions.description: Whether the content, depth and reading level match who will read it: their expertise, role and what they need to decide.
judge_asks: Is the reading level right for this reader's expertise?
Does it answer the question this reader is asking?
Is it about what they care about?

rubric.1: Poor fit in level or focus.
rubric.4: Feels written for this reader alone.

extra_dimensions.advice: Write to the reader's level and lead with what they care about; cut background they already know.

example.before: (A technical deep-dive sent to a board member)
example.after: (One page on cost, risk and the decision needed)

extra_dimensions.name: First impression
extra_dimensions.description: Whether the opening earns the next line: specific, reader-focused, and free of throat-clearing.
judge_asks: Would the reader keep going after the first sentence?
Is the opening about them, and specific?
Is there any throat-clearing to cut?

rubric.0: Opens with filler or the writer's biography.
rubric.4: An opening the reader can't ignore.

extra_dimensions.advice: Open with the reader's situation, a specific fact or the big idea; cut greetings-as-content and background.

example.before: I hope this email finds you well. My name is Tom and I work at BrightPath.
example.after: Your Q3 update mentioned the cloud migration twice.

extra_dimensions.name: Assumed knowledge
extra_dimensions.description: Whether the text assumes knowledge the reader may not have: undefined acronyms, insider jargon, missing context.
judge_asks: Are acronyms and terms defined at first use?
Is there insider jargon this reader won't know?
Is any essential context missing?

rubric.4: Perfectly pitched; nothing to look up.

extra_dimensions.advice: Spell out acronyms at first use, swap jargon for plain terms, and add one line of context where the reader might be lost.

example.before: Our MLOps CoE will uplift your TCO via KPIs.
example.after: Our machine-learning team will cut the total cost of running your models.

extra_dimensions.name: Inclusive language
extra_dimensions.description: Whether the language welcomes every reader: no gendered defaults, ableist idioms or assumptions about age, background or ability.
judge_asks: Is there gendered or exclusionary language?
Are there idioms that could alienate some readers?
Would every intended reader feel addressed?

rubric.4: Warmly inclusive without drawing attention to itself.

extra_dimensions.advice: Replace gendered defaults (chairman, manpower, guys) and ableist idioms (crazy, lame, tone-deaf) with neutral, precise words.

example.before: Hey guys, the chairman thinks this plan is insane.
example.after: Hi everyone, the chair thinks this plan is very ambitious.

extra_dimensions.name: Explicit or implicit
extra_dimensions.description: Low-context cultures want things spelled out; high-context cultures read between the lines and find over-explanation patronising.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Explicit' and 'Implicit'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Explicit: say it plainly, summarise, repeat the point. Implicit: suggest more than you state; trust shared understanding.

poles.low: Explicit: say it plainly, summarise, repeat the point.
poles.high: Implicit: suggest more than you state; trust shared understanding.

extra_dimensions.name: Direct or indirect
extra_dimensions.description: How bluntly asks, disagreement and bad news are expressed.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Direct' and 'Indirect'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Direct: state the ask and any problem plainly. Indirect: soften asks and criticism; use questions, conditionals and context.

poles.low: Direct: state the ask and any problem plainly.
poles.high: Indirect: soften asks and criticism; use questions, conditionals and context.

extra_dimensions.name: Applications-first or principles-first
extra_dimensions.description: Whether readers want the practical point first, or the reasoning and principles first.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Applications-first' and 'Principles-first'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Applications-first: lead with the conclusion and examples, then why. Principles-first: build the reasoning before the recommendation.

poles.low: Applications-first: lead with the conclusion and examples, then why.
poles.high: Principles-first: build the reasoning before the recommendation.

extra_dimensions.name: Informal or formal
extra_dimensions.description: Expected register and deference, linked to power distance.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Informal' and 'Formal'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Informal: first names, contractions and a level tone are fine. Formal: titles, courteous openings and closings, respect for seniority.

poles.low: Informal: first names, contractions and a level tone are fine.
poles.high: Formal: titles, courteous openings and closings, respect for seniority.

extra_dimensions.name: Task or relationship
extra_dimensions.description: Whether trust is built through competence and results, or through relationship and rapport.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Task' and 'Relationship'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Task: lead with credentials, results and specifics. Relationship: invest in rapport, shared connections and long-term partnership before the business.

poles.low: Task: lead with credentials, results and specifics.
poles.high: Relationship: invest in rapport, shared connections and long-term partnership before the business.

extra_dimensions.name: Individual or group
extra_dimensions.description: Whether benefits are framed for the individual reader or for their group, team and family.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Individual' and 'Group'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Individual: personal benefit, choice and achievement. Group: team benefit, harmony, shared success and what peers do.

poles.low: Individual: personal benefit, choice and achievement.
poles.high: Group: team benefit, harmony, shared success and what peers do.

extra_dimensions.name: Deadline or long-term
extra_dimensions.description: How time and urgency are framed: now and deadlines, or patience and the long run.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Deadline' and 'Long-term'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Deadline: clear dates, quick wins, a reason to act now. Long-term: patience, lasting value, relationships over years; urgency can feel pushy.

poles.low: Deadline: clear dates, quick wins, a reason to act now.
poles.high: Long-term: patience, lasting value, relationships over years; urgency can feel pushy.

extra_dimensions.name: Brief or detailed
extra_dimensions.description: Appetite for detail, process and guarantees before deciding.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Brief' and 'Detailed'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Brief: headline and essentials; detail on request. Detailed: process, specifics, guarantees and risk mitigation up front.

poles.low: Brief: headline and essentials; detail on request.
poles.high: Detailed: process, specifics, guarantees and risk mitigation up front.

extra_dimensions.name: Restrained or expressive
extra_dimensions.description: How much emotion, enthusiasm and exclamation readers expect or tolerate.
judge_asks: Where does the text sit between 'Restrained' and 'Expressive'?
Where does this reader's culture expect it to sit?
What would close the gap?

rubric.0: Badly mismatched to the reader's culture.
rubric.4: Feels native to the reader's culture.

extra_dimensions.advice: Restrained: understated, factual, calm. Expressive: warmth, enthusiasm and personal feeling are welcome.

poles.high: Expressive: warmth, enthusiasm and personal feeling are welcome.

extra_dimensions.name: Idioms and references
extra_dimensions.description: Culture-bound idioms, sports metaphors, humour and references that may not travel or translate.
judge_asks: Are there idioms or references a non-native or foreign reader might miss?
Would humour land in this culture?
Would the text survive translation?

rubric.0: Full of references that won't travel.
rubric.4: Travels cleanly to any reader.

extra_dimensions.advice: Swap idioms and sports metaphors for literal phrasing; keep humour gentle and universal.

example.before: Let's touch base and see if we can hit a home run on this.
example.after: Let's speak next week and see if we can make this a real success.

culture.note: Lewis placements are HowDoesThisLand's estimates of each country's blend of the three poles. Hofstede figures are approximate published country scores (mostly 2010 dataset). Expected positions on the nine text scales are derived from both, plus an estimate of persuasion style. Countries contain many cultures; treat every profile as a starting point, not a stereotype.

poles.name: Linear-active
poles.summary: Task-focused, planned, punctual, direct. Trusts facts and procedures.
poles.writing: Lead with the point and the facts. Be concise, specific and punctual about dates. Directness reads as honesty.
poles.examples: Germany, Switzerland, the US, the Netherlands

poles.name: Multi-active
poles.summary: People-focused, expressive, flexible with time, does several things at once. Trusts relationships.
poles.writing: Invest in warmth and the relationship. Personal tone, story and enthusiasm help. Rigid deadlines and cold efficiency can read as distant.
poles.examples: Italy, Spain, Latin America, much of the Middle East

poles.name: Reactive
poles.summary: Listening-focused, courteous, indirect, values harmony and face. Trusts courtesy and consistency.
poles.writing: Be courteous and modest. Avoid pressure, blunt criticism and overclaiming. Give context and leave room to respond. Silence is not disagreement.
poles.examples: Japan, China, Finland, much of East Asia

hofstede_dims.name: Power distance
hofstede_dims.high: Expect formality, titles and deference to seniority.
hofstede_dims.low: Flat and informal; first names are fine.

hofstede_dims.name: Individualism
hofstede_dims.low: Frame group benefit, harmony and what peers do.

hofstede_dims.name: Achievement and success
hofstede_dims.low: Cooperation, care and quality of life motivate; boasting backfires.

hofstede_dims.name: Uncertainty avoidance
hofstede_dims.high: Give detail, process, guarantees and risk mitigation.
hofstede_dims.low: Keep it brief and open; too much procedure feels rigid.

hofstede_dims.name: Indulgence
hofstede_dims.high: Enjoyment, optimism and fun land well.
hofstede_dims.low: Restraint and duty land better than fun.

scales.name: Explicit or implicit
scales.low: Explicit: say it plainly, summarise, repeat the point.
scales.high: Implicit: suggest more than you state; trust shared understanding.

scales.name: Direct or indirect
scales.low: Direct: state the ask and any problem plainly.
scales.high: Indirect: soften asks and criticism; use questions, conditionals and context.

scales.name: Applications-first or principles-first
scales.low: Applications-first: lead with the conclusion and examples, then why.
scales.high: Principles-first: build the reasoning before the recommendation.

scales.name: Informal or formal
scales.low: Informal: first names, contractions and a level tone are fine.
scales.high: Formal: titles, courteous openings and closings, respect for seniority.

scales.name: Task or relationship
scales.low: Task: lead with credentials, results and specifics.
scales.high: Relationship: invest in rapport, shared connections and long-term partnership before the business.

scales.name: Individual or group
scales.low: Individual: personal benefit, choice and achievement.
scales.high: Group: team benefit, harmony, shared success and what peers do.

scales.name: Deadline or long-term
scales.low: Deadline: clear dates, quick wins, a reason to act now.
scales.high: Long-term: patience, lasting value, relationships over years; urgency can feel pushy.

scales.name: Brief or detailed
scales.low: Brief: headline and essentials; detail on request.
scales.high: Detailed: process, specifics, guarantees and risk mitigation up front.

scales.name: Restrained or expressive
scales.high: Expressive: warmth, enthusiasm and personal feeling are welcome.

culture.weight_effect: Reader culture nudges the appeal weights: linear-active readers weight logos more; multi-active readers weight pathos more; reactive readers weight ethos (courtesy, consistency, credibility) more and kairos (pressure) less.
